sections.title: Quality Planning
sections.en: 3.6.3 Quality Planning The following sections will cover settings and options that you’ll find in the quality planning configuration menu of QM. Defect Classes You may have different types of defect classes, such as critical or minor defects. You can categorize the defects into different catalog types, such as quality defects or plant maintenance defects. The SAP system characterizes defects into five different defect class categories. You can choose to work with the defaults for defect classes or create new ones. To create defect classes, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Catalog  Define Defect Classes. Figure 3.89 shows an overview of various defect classes. Choose Dfct Class 01 1 so that the detailed view of the defect appears 2. The system displays the Quality Score. The critical or more severe a defect, the lower the quality score. Together with the quality score in a defect class, the system uses characteristic weighting to come up with an overall quality score of an inspection lot, which forms the basis of supplier evaluation. The system calculates the quality score based on the following equation: Quality score = Quality score in defect class × Characteristic weighting ÷ Sum total of all characteristic weightage Batch Valuation Without Material Spec. Checkbox that requires characteristics in a batch to be directly synchronized with material specifications so that results recording can be successfully performed. This option is helpful when you want to transfer inspection results to batch classification. See Section 3.2.4, where we put this option to use. Field Details Table 3.8 Inspection Lot Completion (Cont.) © 203 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection Figure 3.89 Defect Classes If you select the Defect Class Allowed checkbox, the system offers the provision to enter a defect class with defect codes, even though you’ve marked the valuation of the characteristic as accepted. In other words, even the accepted master inspection charac- teristic can still have defects, and this checkbox provides the necessary option to note the same. Not choosing the checkbox only enables you to choose a defect class when you have a rejected valuation of a characteristic. The Next Functions in Results Recording area allows you to include the Workflow Link, Activation Q-Notif., or No Next Function (or follow-up function) after recording a defect class. Define Defect Categories With the define defect categories feature, you can define customer-specific defect cate- gories for defects recording. The defect category controls the following settings:  Using a customer-specific defect category, you can specify the task type for a defect. The task type determines, for example, whether a follow-up action can be assigned to a task in a defect.  You can add context-specific fields for a defect category. This requires knowledge of SAP Fiori elements.  You can select defects of a customer-specific defect category via their defect cate- gory in the Process Defects app. To define a defect category, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Non- conformance Management  Defects Recording  Define Defect Categories. 3 Quality Inspection 204 Catalogs In the context of quality planning and quality inspection, the term catalog refers to a collection of unique keys that describe a subject, both in the positive and the negative sense. A catalog is a group of codes that you normally use to categorize different aspects and activities of QM (and PM) and include defects, causes, tasks, actions, or usage decisions. An example of a catalog of defects can be defect codes, which contain all the possible defects of electrical or mechanical parts of the machinery. In the SAP S/4HANA system implementation project, designing the defect catalogs and other catalogs often takes significant time and effort because the existing catalog struc- tures in the enterprise have to be migrated to a schema that suits the QM area. There- fore, the most frequently occurring problem isn’t missing catalogs, but rather the sheer number of catalogs and the fact that problem descriptions often overlap. The better- suited and practical approach of classifying problem descriptions in catalogs according to defect location, defect type, and defect cause also often causes uncertainty with assigning the corresponding codes. The following sections will discuss the various standard catalog types available in the SAP S/4HANA system. Although standard catalog types available are generally suffi- cient to meet most business needs, new catalog types can also be configured. Each cat- alog type has specific codes that are then used in the business processes. Further, each code within a catalog type provides an option to perform subsequent follow-on func- tions too. Catalog Types You can select the defaults for catalog types or add additional ones if there is a business need. To view the available catalog types, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Manage- ment  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Catalog Types. Figure 3.90 shows the initial screen of catalog types. You must not change SAP catalog types 1–9. However, you can create new catalog types within the P–Z range. The following catalog types are available in the SAP S/4HANA system:  Catalog type 0: Action reasons This catalog type is specific defects recording wherein specific action can be assigned when a defect is first identified and recording.  Catalog type 1: Characteristic attributes This catalog type is specific to results recording and is for defining qualitative char- acteristics. It has special importance in the catalog system. One reason for this is that you can maintain both OK and NOK definitions here; another is that you can only assess the catalog entries only via selected sets. If you’re using a rejected-defect class for supplier evaluation, you have to enter a defect class (major defect, minor defect, etc.). Rejecting defect classes are by nature the same as the defect types (defects) and are structured in the same way. If a qualitative characteristic has been created in the © 205 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection inspection plan, the valuation always uses a code from the selected set of the charac- teristic attributes.  Catalog type 2: Tasks You use this catalog to store the tasks that are necessary in the context of quality notifications. Examples of typical tasks can include supplier visit, test equipment calibration, construction change, or a process-capability test. You can also activate automatic follow-up action functions here.  Catalog type 3: Usage decisions The system uses this special catalog type only for inspection lot completions. You can only access this via selected sets. Every code in the selected set has further con- trol functions that you can use to accept or reject valuation: – Valuation (lot decision) – Quality score – Follow-on action  Catalog type 4: Events This catalog type contains events for PM.  Catalog type 5: Causes This catalog type is also used in quality notifications. Typical defect causes include, for example, tool breakage, incorrect storage, transport damage, and incorrect deliv- ery specification. Figure 3.90 Catalog Types 3 Quality Inspection 206  Catalog type 6: Effects This catalog type contains the consequences of defects for PM.  Catalog type 7: Hold This catalog type contains the reasons to hold for PM.  Catalog type 8: Activities (QM) You define the actions to take as a result of measures. We recommend that you use only measures in the quality notifications because it’s usually difficult to make a clear logical distinction between measures and actions.  Catalog type 9: Defect types As with the characteristic attributes, you can assign defect classes to this catalog type.  Catalog type A: Activities (PM) This catalog type contains the activities catalog for PM.  Catalog type B: Object parts This catalog type contains the object parts catalog for PM.  Catalog type C: Overview of damage This catalog type contains the damage catalog for PM.  Catalog type D: Coding This catalog type contains the general description that is used as the title or subject of messages (error message, problem message, complaint, etc.). These entries are also the titles for the error-description text.  Catalog type E: Defect locations The catalog structure is the same as the general definition.  Catalog type F: Decision – SPM return The catalog structure contains decision codes that the user can choose from while deciding to return special machinery to the supplier (SPM). Tips and Tricks When the system displays the catalog entries in the results recording or in the quality notifications, only the description of the code with its short text and key are visible. If you also want the system to display the associated code group, enter “&” (an amper- sand) in the code group text. The system inserts the code text into the code group text in place of the & symbol. To edit a catalog, follow menu path Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspec- tion Lot Completion  Edit Code Groups and Codes for Usage Decisions. Figure 3.91 shows catalog 3 for usage decisions with code group 01. Within each code group, you maintain individual codes and their descriptions. © 207 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection Figure 3.91 Catalog Type for Usage Decisions Catalog Hierarchy The catalog hierarchy usually has three levels, but in the case of catalogs with selected sets, it has four. These are catalog types 1 (characteristic attributes) and 3 (usage deci- sions), and they have an extra hierarchy level, known as selected sets. You can use this extra level to group subsets of a code group according to higher criteria. In addition, you assign an Accept or Reject valuation to every code in a selected set. You can also assign a follow-up action to the individual codes. To edit a selected set for usage decisions, follow menu path Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspection Lot Completion  Edit Selected Sets for Usage Decisions. Figure 3.92 shows catalog 3 (usage decisions) for plant 1710 and selected set 04 (goods receipt). Notice that the first column is the code group of selected set 03, whereas the second column is the individual code within the selected set. Each code of a selected set can have a valuation code, such as Accepted (OK), Rejected (not OK), or Not Valuated. In the Quality Score column, you can assign a quality score that is associated with each code of a selected set. Referring to the Posting in UD column for a specific usage deci- sion code of a selected set, you can leverage the system to automatically propose and then take a necessary action based on the specific usage decision code for the selected set for usage decisions. Figure 3.93 offers various options for Posting in UD that are directly associated with the specific code of the selected set. Tips and Tricks Remember that you can assign UD Selected Set and its corresponding plant in an inspection type so that during a usage decision, the system brings up only the relevant usage decision codes for you to choose from. Refer to Section 3.4 for more information. 3 Quality Inspection 208 Figure 3.92 Selected Set Figure 3.93 Stock Posting Options in Selected Set Define Default Values for Control Indicators The control indicator saves a significant amount of time and effort during master inspection characteristic creation. During master inspection characteristic creation, the user needs to select certain checkboxes. However, creating a control indicator and then assigning it in a master inspection characteristic automatically enables all check- box options. While creating master inspection characteristics, look for the Preset Indicators field, and then enter the code there. © 209 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection To define default values for control indicators, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteristic, Inspection Method  Define Default Values for Control Indicators. Figure 3.94 shows the default values indicator control key (IndCKey) 3010, where the right side shows the characteris- tic control indicators. After you’ve made the necessary settings here, another popup appears that allows you to incorporate more default values for the characteristic. You assign this indicator control key 3010 while creating a characteristic. Figure 3.94 Control Indicators Define Characteristic Weighing The system uses the characteristic weighing to calculate quality scores. A characteristic with a critical defect will have a higher weight factor and will eventually have greater impact on the quality scores calculation. In other words, a critical defect will lower the quality score of the inspection lot. During results recording, if you record several defects of an inspection lot, then the system multiplies each defect class’s score with the weight factor to calculate an overall quality score for the inspection lot. 3 Quality Inspection 210 You can create characteristic weighing together with the weight factor by following menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteristic, Inspection Method  Define Characteristic Weighing. In the screen that appears, choose Char. Wght 01, and the screen in Figure 3.95 appears. Checking the No Skip Allowed checkbox ensures that, on selection of defect Critical Characteristic or Charac. Weight 01, the system doesn’t allow inspection skips in results recording. Figure 3.95 Characteristic Weighting Define Inspector Qualification An inspector qualification stipulates that a specific person or group requires the neces- sary qualification to conduct the quality tests. Inspection qualification is for informa- tion purposes only. It’s not a control function that can stop users from performing a specific action. To define inspector qualification, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteristic, Inspection Method  Define Inspector Qualification. Define Tolerance Key The tolerance key defines the tolerance range for the quantitative characteristic. When the results of an inspection characteristic fall within the tolerance key/range, it’s viewed as acceptable for the purpose of valuating the characteristic. To create or change a tolerance key, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteristic, Inspection Method  Define Tolerance Key. The screen that appears consists of a long list of industry-standard toler- ance keys that you can evaluate before proceeding to create new ones. Choose Toler. Key (tolerance key) A10, and then choose Details to pen the screen in Figure 3.96. Here, you can control the number of decimal places, as well as define the unit of mea- sure of the tolerance key. You can also set and copy the Target Value while creating a characteristic. Choose Nominal Values in the screen in Figure 3.96 to go to the screen in Figure 3.97 where you can define both upper and lower nominal, specification, and limit values, including the number of decimal places for each. © 211 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection Figure 3.96 Tolerance Key Figure 3.97 Details of Tolerance Key A10 Define the Estimation Procedure for Fraction of Defects In this step, you can define your own procedure to estimate the percentage of defective material using the characteristic inspection results. The following are the fraction esti- mates: 3 Quality Inspection 212  Nonconforming units (with regard to a characteristic and in the inspection lot)  Characteristic values outside of the tolerance range The keys for the procedure are defined in the inspection characteristic. The system maintains fraction estimates for the following distributions:  Binomial distribution The system uses binomial distribution when there are exactly two mutually exclu- sive outcomes of a result. The outcome is either a success or a failure.  Poisson distribution The Poisson distribution uses the model of number of events occurring within a given time interval.  Normal distribution Mean and standard deviations are taken into account in a sample’s results. To define an estimation procedure for a fraction of defects, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteristic, Inspec- tion Method  Define Estimation Procedure for Fraction of Defects. In Figure 3.98, you can define your own estimation procure and assign the relevant function module. Figure 3.98 Share Estimate for Inspection Characteristics Number Ranges You can define your own number ranges for inspection characteristics and inspection methods. To do this, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Plan- ning  Basic Data  Inspection Characteristic, Inspection Method  Define Number Range for Inspection Characteristics. © 213 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection The initial screen for Number Range for Inspection Characteristics appears. To add a number range, choose Insert, and in the popup that appears, enter the identification number (No), and then define the number range in From No. and To Number. You can have internal and external number assignments. For the external number assignment option, select the Ext checkbox. Note The basics of creating and assigning number ranges are the same, so you can use the information in this section to create and assign them in other QM master data setups. Inspection for Goods Movements If you want to control inspection at procurement or transfer, you need to define it in this configuration step. The SAP system has already defined this for standard move- ment types. Only if you create a new movement type do you need to add it here. You also need to make sure the inspection type is assigned to the inspection lot origin. Fur- ther, if you want to control automatic creation of inspection lots for any movement types, you can activate/deactivate them. To make the necessary settings for inspection for goods movements, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Inspection Lot Creation  Inspec- tion for Goods Movement. In the popup that appears, choose Update Control, and then enter your custom-defined movement type. Choose Back, and when the popup reap- pears, choose Deactivate Quality Inspection for a Movement Type. This leads to Figure 3.99 where you can deactivate the QM function for any movement type(s) by selecting the QM not active checkbox for the relevant movement type. Figure 3.99 Deactivating QM for Movement Type 3 Quality Inspection 214 Note In Appendix A, you’ll find a list of several movement types and associated inspection origins. You can use that list to integrate QM into as many business processes as neces- sary to meet your business needs. Adapt Rules for Sample Determination If the standard sampling procedure doesn’t fulfill your company’s business needs, then you can assign additional or different rules by assigning a specific function module to the sample determination rule. Use the menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sample, SPC  Define Sampling Determination  Adapt Rules for Sample Determination. Define Valuation Mode Valuation mode enables the system to valuate inspection characteristics based on whether the mode of valuation will be manual or automatic and is for attributive (qual- itative) or variable (quantitative) characteristics. When you’re creating a sampling pro- cedure, you need to choose the relevant valuation mode that’s directly linked to the valuation rule. Let’s explain this with an example. Consider valuation mode 110 (Attr. Insp. Nonconforming Units/Manual), which con- tains valuation rule 111 (Attr. Insp. Nonconforming Units/Manual). The combination of valuation mode 110 and valuation rule 11 means that the system decides to accept or reject an attributive (qualitative) characteristic based on how many of the inspected samples of an inspection characteristic fail. For example, say that the total number of samples inspected is 20 units, and you record 3 units as rejected due to defects or non- conformance. Whether that characteristic passes or fails depends on the formula used for valuation rule 11 or function module QEBR_NONCONFORM_UNIT_OR_MANUAL. You’ve defined the actual number of samples allowed for pass or fail in the sampling proce- dure. In this specific case, though the system automatically valuates the characteristic as either accepted or rejected, it also provides an option for the user to manually valu- ate or overrule the automatic valuation. This option to perform manual valuation (despite the system’s automatic valuation) isn’t available if you use valuation rule 10. To summarize, a few valuation modes are valuation by number of defects, number of nonconforming units, or defect code, and they are for attributive or variable character- istics with the option of automatic, manual, or both valuation controls of an inspection characteristic. Tips and Tricks If the characteristic is quantitative, then choose a valuation mode in the sampling pro- cedure as one of the variable types. © 215 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection If the characteristic is qualitative, then choose a valuation mode in the sampling proce- dure as one of the attribute types. To navigate to the valuation mode, use menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sampling, SPC  Define Valuation Rules. In the screen that appears, choose Valuation Mode 100. You’ll see a screen that shows valuation mode 100 for attributive (qualitative) inspec- tion by number of nonconforming (or number of defects) units, with valuation rule 10 assigned to valuation mode 100. Define Valuation Rule To set up or navigate to a valuation rule, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sample, SPC  Define Sampling Determination. In the popup that appears, choose Modify Valuation Rule, and then from the list of various available valu- ation modes, choose Valuation Rule 10. This leads to the screen in Figure 3.100, wherein the system uses the function module to valuate a characteristic. Figure 3.100 Valuation Rules 3 Quality Inspection 216 If you have any unique business need to valuate a characteristic that’s not available in the standard system offering, then you can create a function module and assign it in this step. Statistical Process Control Organizations use the statistical process control as a tool to improve product quality by reducing process variations. There are two sources of process variation:  Chance variation (later renamed to common cause variation) that is inherent in the process, stable over time, and assignable  Uncontrolled variation (later renamed to special cause variation), which is unstable over time—the result of specific events outside the system Control charts attempt to distinguish between these two types of process variation:  Common cause variation, which is intrinsic to the process and will always be present  Special cause variation, which stems from external sources, indicates that the pro- cess is out of statistical control, and needs evaluation on a case-by-case basis When you create an inspection characteristic, you select the SPC checkbox to let the sys- tem know that you’ll be monitoring this specific characteristic through the statistical process control. In addition, remember to simultaneously select the Sampling Proce- dure checkbox; otherwise, the system deactivates the SPC checkbox that you previously selected. Later, when you assign this statistical process control characteristic to an inspection plan, the system prompts you to enter the sampling procedure, as well as the statistical process control criteria. To navigate to the statistical process control criteria settings, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sampling, SPC  Statistical Process Control  Define SPC Criteria. In Figure 3.101, you’ll find several combinations of task list characteristics that align with the material, supplier, customer, and even equip- ment or the functional location of PM. Choose SPC Crit. 010 1, and the details appears on the screen on the right 2. Usage is the option to select a specific task list to use the statistical process control cri- teria. In addition, the radio buttons enable selection of the assignment of the control chart either on every inspection lot or at every inspection point. Note See Chapter 19 on quality control to understand how to leverage statistical process control to improve your business processes. © 217 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection Figure 3.101 Statistical Process Control Criteria Define Control Chart Type Control charts are most commonly used in the production area. Your system comes with several preset sampling procedures for statistical process control inspection planning. To define your own statistical process control sampling procedure in the SAP S/4HANA system, proceed exactly as you would for the lot inspection. The sam- pling procedure input mask contains one extra attribute: the indicator for the inspec- tion point. The inspection point control object allows you to set the inspection 3 Quality Inspection 218 interval—that is, whether the inspection is to be container-based, time-interval- based, or event-based. Define the following first:  Sample type Only a fixed sample is allowed.  Valuation mode Select the special valuation mode, statistical process control inspection. With this setting, valuations of samples or characteristics use the action limits of the quality control chart. A rejection occurs if the action limits are violated. If there aren’t yet enough measurement values to calculate an action limit, the procedure switches to manual calculation until the measured values are sufficient.  Control chart type You have to assign a control chart type for statistical process control sampling pro- cedures. When you do so, the system checks whether the sampling procedure will use inspection points or independent multiple samples. With independent multiple samples, control chart types with samples are allowed; otherwise, control chart types without samples are allowed. In control charts with memory (moving average chart, mean-value chart, or moving- range chart), the control variable isn’t restricted to the current sample. These control chart tracks don’t support the statistical process control inspection valuation mode. When defining the sample size, there are some quality aspects that you have to take into account. If you want to use the sample size n = 1, you should ensure the following:  There is no S track in the control chart you intend to use.  The overall dispersion, and not the internal dispersion, is used to calculate the pro- cess dispersion in the calculations for the action limits. The reason for this is that in samples with the size n = 1, the standard deviation is always 0. Tips and Tricks In statistical process control inspections with measured recording, sample sizes from 3 to 10 are normal, with n = 5 the most commonly used value. For quantitative characteristics, the original values of which don’t have a normal distri- bution, you can select a larger sample size to use the central specification limit set of the statistics, whereby the distribution of the mean values is almost normal. You can then use Shewhart charts for the mean value, even if the distribution of the population isn’t normal. The more the distribution deviates from the norm, the greater the sample size should be. The statistical process control criteria determine the update process for the control chart and are controlled by function modules. Before the system creates a new control © 219 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection chart (during results recording), this system checks whether a suitable chart already exists. The function modules are well documented and can be easily adapted to suit your own needs. It’s also a simple matter to create a control chart for a characteristic or supplier only. The standard SAP system already contains the following function modules:  QRKS_CHARACTERISTIC: Control chart for characteristics  QRKS_INSPECTION_LOT: Control chart for characteristics or inspection lots  QRKS_MATERIAL: Control chart for characteristics or materials  QRKS_MATERIAL_CUSTOMER: Control chart for characteristics, materials, or customers  QRKS_MATERIAL_MANUFACTURER: Control chart for characteristics, materials, or manu- facturers  QRKS_MATERIAL_SOLD_TO_PARTY: Control chart for characteristics, materials, or sold- to parties  QRKS_MATERIAL_VENDOR: Control chart for characteristics, materials, or suppliers  QRKS_MATERIAL_WORK_CENTER: Control chart for characteristics, materials, or work centers  QRKS_PURCHASING_DOCUMENT: Control chart for characteristics or purchasing docu- ments  QRKS_SALES_ORDER: Control chart for characteristics or sales orders Statistical process control defines which charts are available, how you process them, and how you assign them to the processes. To define or make changes to the control settings of a control chart, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sampling, SPC  Statis- tical Process Control  Define Control Chart Type. On the initial screen that appears, first choose Ctrl Chart Type “110”, and then choose Details (not shown) and the screen in Figure 3.102 appears. Figure 3.103 shows the control chart type 110, Shewhart chart for x-Bar. Here, you can control when the system actually creates a new control chart. Choose Simulate, and the system displays the appropriate chart in the lower half of the screen. Referring again to Figure 3.102, this time choose Control chart tracks on the left side, which leads to the screen in Figure 3.104. This screen shows the system-suggested upper and lower warning and action limits for numeric parameters. You can choose to optionally or always display these limits in the control chart. The system calculates and displays all limits, but after choosing the Change Control Limits checkbox (not shown, but will be visible when scrolled further down in Figure 3.104), you can also manually enter the control limits, and the system clearly identifies them too. 3 Quality Inspection 220 After basic data is set up, you need to set up inspection planning data. Inspection plan- ning consists of two subcomponents: general (applies for all operations) and operation- specific. Quality inspection uses task list type Q. Quality inspection integrates with production-related task list types, such as routings, rate routings, and master recipes, or a reference operation set can also be used. Figure 3.102 Control Chart Overview Figure 3.103 Control Chart: Detailed Settings © 221 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection Figure 3.104 Control Chart Tracks Assign Task List Types to Material Types The SAP system has many standard material types that already form the combination with task list inspection type Q. However, if you’ve created any new material type that will have quality implications, then you need to ensure that the necessary configura- tion is in place; otherwise, the system prevents you from creating the inspection plan (task list type Q—inspection plan). Figure 3.105 Assignment of Material Type to Task List Type 3 Quality Inspection 222 To assign task list types to material types, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Manage- ment  Quality Planning  Inspection Planning  General  Assign Task List Types to Mate- rial Types. In the screen that appears, choose Maintain Parameters for Task List Type, which leads to the screen in Figure 3.105. There, check the task list type (TLType) “Q” and material type (MTyp) combination. Planner Group Planner groups are used to group activities, typically in PM, PP, or supply planning pro- cesses. In QM, you configure and assign planner groups in task lists. Planner groups eventually help in reporting, when you want to see task list(s) of specific planner groups. To create a planner group, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Inspection Planning  General  Define Planner Group. Define an Identifier for Inspection Points You can define an identifier for inspection points for physical samples, partial lots in production, and maintenance objects (e.g., equipment or functional locations). A con- figured identifier for the inspection point then needs to be filled with relevant informa- tion before you can record the results of an inspection lot or an inspection point. To create or change the identifier for an inspection point, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Inspection Planning  General  Define Identi- fier for Inspection Points. Figure 3.106 shows field combination 300 and inspection point type (InspPt type) 1, Inspection Point for Equipment. The right dropdown shows the various available inspection point types. When you’re creating an inspection point identifier, it’s important to choose InspPt type to denote the specific use inspection point. The inspection points available are as follows:  (blank): Freely defined inspection point  1: Inspection point for equipment  2: Inspection point for functional location  3: Inspection point for physical sample You can define up to six user fields, with the flexibility to define the user field’s text per the business need. For example, a user field can be titled “Shift” and have the field for- mat Number, and the field length is three numeric values. You can control the display positions of the six user fields by defining the numbering of the display order in the Field Act. option. If the Shift field must be displayed for data entry at position number 2, then you need to number Field Act. as “2.” © 223 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection Figure 3.106 Inspection Point If you select the Last Inspected Sample Is Valuated checkbox, the results for the last inspected inspection point are valid. All characteristic results for previous inspection points are automatically set to invalid. Only the results for the last inspection point are considered for summarization at the summarized characteristic level. Tips and Tricks You should set this indicator if samples should be drawn (and inspection points cre- ated) until the target value is reached. On the Valuation tab, you can set the default options for valuating inspection points and assigning codes and code groups to facilitate the data entry efforts during results recording. On the Function modules tab, you can either use the preset or predefined function modules or assign your own custom-defined function module. Alternatively, you can simply deactivate this by deselecting the Use Func Component checkbox. Inspection-Characteristic Origin You can define a unique identifier to denote the origin of inspection characteristics so that when you use them in an inspection plan, you know the origin of the characteristic. 3 Quality Inspection 224 For example, in Chapter 16 on FMEA and the control plan, you copy an inspection char- acteristic undergoing the FMEA process into an inspection plan. When you do this, the system asks you for the characteristic’s origin and brings up the list that you define in this configuration step. To create or change an inspection-characteristic origin, follow menu path SAP IMG  Qual- ity Management  Quality Planning  Inspection Planning  Operation  Inspection Charac- teristic  Define Inspection-Characteristic Origin. In the resulting screen, you can define a numeric origin, together with the description of inspection-characteristic origin. Engineering Workbench The Engineering Workbench facilitates the modification or updating of a large number of QM master data and associated objects to save time and reduce the chances of data entry error. You can either create a new working area or modify the existing ones to meet your business needs. A working area makes available all the different fields and options that you’ll use while using the Engineering Workbench. To access the Engineering Workbench, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Manage- ment  Quality Planning  Engineering Workbench  Define Work Areas. Choose Working Area Q_OPR_000000000010, which leads to the screen in Figure 3.107. Figure 3.107 Engineering Workbench: Details © 225 3.6 Configuration Basics: Quality Planning and Quality Inspection You can select various radio buttons and checkboxes to ensure that the system dis- plays only the relevant information while working in the Engineering Workbench. You can also set a lock in the Lock Automatically section at the relevant level (header or operation) to prevent anyone from making changes in the inspection plan while another user is working in the Engineering Workbench. Notice that you can activate Classification (see Chapter 9 on batch management, which also covers classification) and see the classes and their associated characteristics. The Object dependencies find greater usage when you’re using the variant configuration functionality or even the advanced classification functionality. When you complete an inspection lot after the completion of a physical inspection, you may or may not make the usage decision. You’re determining the quality valuation and updating the quality level. If you have links to a batch class, you can transfer inspection results to batch specifications. Based on the usage decision, the system can perform follow-up actions. Note that short-term and long-term inspection completion are two separate steps. For short-term inspection, you need to enter the results before making the usage decision. For long-term inspection, you can enter the results even after the usage decision has been made for an inspection lot.
