sections.title: Storage Conditions
sections.en: 15.3.8 Storage Conditions Because the inspection lot for the initial test was successful as well as approved, the next step is to specify the storage condition(s) to keep the physical samples in. In Action Box, choose Specify Storage Conditions. In the screen in Figure 15.15, enter the sample quantity for each storage condition. Figure 15.15 Define Storage Conditions of Stability Samples In this example, enter a sample quantity of 1 PC; each is stored in Stor.Cond. (the first column to the left) 00000001 with the text “Room Temperature 21°”, and in Stor.Cond. 00000002 with the text “Temperature 20°”. In addition, notice that the physical sam- ple 900000026 now has the REL (for released) status. Select both Stor.Cond. 00000001 and Stor.Cond. 00000002, and choose Save and Change Notification. Note Storage conditions are covered in Section 15.4.3. You must carefully evaluate all the storage conditions that you’ll need for the stability study, and ensure their availability accordingly. 15 Stability Study 664 The following sections discuss the storage conditions and storage locations associated with a stability study. Specify Additional Storage Condition You can define additional storage conditions if there is any such need during the stabil- ity study. Choose Specify Add. Storage Conds in Action Box to arrive at the screen in Figure 15.16. Figure 15.16 Defining Additional Storage Conditions Here, you have the option to incorporate an additional storage condition for your sam- ples for the stability study. When you’ve made the necessary changes, choose Save and Change Notification. In this example, we enter the sample location shown in Figure 15.16. Store Stability Samples To formally begin the stability study process, you need to store the physical samples in the specified storage conditions. On doing so, the system updates the status of physical © 665 15.3 Stability Study for a Material samples to REL (released). With this status of physical samples, the system enables inspection lot creation, as well as all other standard QM activities, such as results recording, defects recording, and usage decision. To place the stability sample in stor- age, and according to chosen storage conditions, choose Store Stability Samples in Action Box to go to Figure 15.17. Figure 15.17 Store Stability Samples in Storage Conditions Here, you update the storage date and sample location, along with the number of labels required for printing. Choose the line item of storage condition 00000001, and then choose Save and Change Notification. Notice that the physical sample at storage condi- tion 00000001 still has the status CRTD. As soon as you save, the system updates the status to REL to release the physical sample. For this example, the physical sample number is 900000027 (the first field shown at the top in Figure 15.16). Use Transaction QPR3 to display physical sample 900000027 and to confirm whether the system updated the information on the physical sample accordingly (see Figure 15.18). Here, the system updates the physical sample’s status to REL and automatically creates inspection lot 160000000007. Because two physical samples were placed in two different storage conditions, the sec- ond physical sample that the system automatically created is 900000028 and the associated inspection lot. 15 Stability Study 666 Figure 15.18 Inspection Lot with Inspection Type 1602 Delete Storage Conditions You can delete a storage condition when you no longer want to continue with a sample placed in a certain storage condition. Choose Delete Storage Conditions in Action Box to go to the screen shown in Figure 15.19. You can, for example, select storage condition 00000002 and choose Delete and Change Notification. Doing so will remove the sam- ple from the stability study. © 667 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.19 Delete Storage Condition

sections.title: Testing Schedule
sections.en: 15.3.9 Testing Schedule If the initial test for the stability study proves satisfactory, then the next step is to cre- ate a testing schedule to monitor the progress or the physical and chemical conditions of the stored samples in the storage conditions over a longer period of time. Setting up a testing schedule enables the system to automatically create inspection lots per the defined schedule to ensure the stability study’s timely results recording and usage decisions. The following sections discuss how to create and change a testing schedule of a stability study and how to complete the testing schedule once the stability study is either com- pleted or isn’t required anymore. Create In Action Box, choose Create Testing Schedule. In Figure 15.20, due to the number range settings, the system internally assigns the Maintenance Plan 700020000002, whereas the maintenance planning category (Maint. plan cat.) ST denotes that it’s applicable to the stability study. A maintenance plan holds and controls all the information related 15 Stability Study 668 to planning and scheduling activities, including automatic creation of inspection lots, on the due dates of inspections. Figure 15.20 Testing Schedule of Inspection for Storage Conditions The maintenance strategy QSTABI is assigned to maintenance plan 700020000002 and is configured to create a new inspection lot every month for the material undergoing the stability study. The Scheduling Period of 1 year (YR) denotes that the stability study will last for one year; the system will create the number of inspection lots accordingly. Finally, in this case, the system creates a monthly inspection lot of inspection type 16, which is the inspection for storage condition. This inspection type compares with inspection type 1601, which was specific to initial sample creation. Note The maintenance plan category is an object that we’ll cover in Section 15.4.7. In addition, because maintenance strategies have extensive use in the PM area of SAP S/4HANA, consider engaging a PM resource to set up the correct maintenance strategy for your stability study. This is an integration point between QM and PM in the stability study. Setting up a maintenance strategy is a business process and not a configuration step, but we’ll cover it in Section 15.4.8 to maintain the ongoing business processes flow and continuity of the stability study in this section. Change You can change the testing schedule of the stability study. This can be helpful when there’s a need to change the testing frequency of the physical samples. You can also use this option to enter any missing or incomplete information in the maintenance plan. © 669 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Choose Change Testing Schedule in Action Box. A popup appears, asking you to con- firm whether you’d like to make changes to the testing schedule. Choose Yes so that the system navigates to the screen in Figure 15.21. Figure 15.21 Maintenance Plan for Changes in Testing Schedule In Figure 15.21, update Group “7” and TL Group Counter “1” in the Inspection Plan area. If you receive an error when doing so, follow these two troubleshooting steps: 1. Use Transaction CWBQM (Engineering Workbench), and in the popup that appears, enter “Q_OPR_000000000010”, which will bring up operations details of the inspection plan. On the screen that appears, enter Material “2234”, Plant “1710”, Task List Type “Q”, Group “7”, and Group Counter “1”, and then choose Load Task Lists from the top menu bar. In the Headers General tab of the screen that appears (see Figure 15.22), assign the maintenance Strategy as “QSTABI”. You’ll have to scroll to the far right of the screen to find this field for assignment. 15 Stability Study 670 2. Select the first operation shown in Figure 15.22, and choose Task Lists  Maintenance Packages, and maintain the monthly packages that belong to Strategy QSTABI, as shown in Figure 15.23. Figure 15.22 Assigning the Maintenance Strategy to the Inspection Plan Figure 15.23 Assigning the Maintenance Package Both these settings in the inspection plan for material 2234 and plant 1710 correspond to the options selected in Figure 15.20 previously. Further, when you’ve made both set- tings in the inspection plan via Transaction CWBQM (the Engineering Workbench) and © 671 15.3 Stability Study for a Material not via the normal inspection plan’s Transaction QP02, where these options aren’t available, you’ll be able to assign group 7 and group counter 1 to the maintenance plan, as shown in Figure 15.22. Tips and Tricks You can also use Transaction IP02 to directly make changes to the maintenance plan (testing schedule). Enter the maintenance plan 700020000002 on the initial screen and press (Enter), and it takes you to Figure 15.21. Furthermore, you can use Transaction IP10 to schedule automatic inspection lot cre- ation, which is relevant for stability studies. On the initial screen of Transaction IP10, enter the relevant maintenance planning category and maintenance strategy. Complete When the testing schedule for the stability study is complete, proceed to update the same so that the system no longer automatically creates inspection lots. Alternatively, you can complete the testing schedule anytime, as deemed necessary. Choose Complete Test Scheduling in Action Box, and a popup appears, asking you to confirm whether you’d like to set the status to Testing Scheduling Completed and return to the stability study. Choose Yes.

sections.title: Inspection Lot for Inspection Type 16
sections.en: 15.3.10 Inspection Lot for Inspection Type 16 With the testing schedule now in place, the system automatically creates inspection lot(s) of inspection type 16 on due date(s). Warning The status of the physical sample is still CRTD (created). Unless the physical sample attains status REL (released), the system doesn’t create inspection lots. To set the phys- ical samples’ status under storage conditions to REL, refer to Section 15.3.2. Figure 15.24 shows the detailed screen of Inspection Lot 160000000006. Notice that this screen has Inspection Type 16, notification 800000004, maintenance plan 700020000002 (not shown but located further down the same screen), and the strat- egy for stability study STABI. The rest of the steps are all the same as in standard QM activities, such as results record- ing and usage decision, and we won’t repeat them here. 15 Stability Study 672 Figure 15.24 Automatic Creation of Inspection Lot by Testing Schedule To check and test whether the system will create the inspection lot per the testing schedule, follow these steps: 1. Store stability samples, as covered in Section 15.3.7, so that the physical samples attain REL status. The system creates inspection lots only for physical samples with the REL status. 2. Use Transaction IP10, and then on the initial screen, enter the maintenance plan. In this example, it’s “700020000002”. 3. On the next screen, choose the Manual Call button to prompt the system to manu- ally trigger inspection lot(s) creation. When the system asks for the date (in a Manual Call field in a popup), enter today’s date, as shown in Figure 15.25. 4. Choose the Scheduled calls tab in Figure 15.26 to see the monthly scheduled mainte- nance calls made. 5. Save your entries and check for the newly created inspection lot using Transaction QA32 for inspection type 16 to bring up the screen in Figure 15.24, shown earlier. © 673 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.25 Start Date of Maintenance Cycle Figure 15.26 Maintenance Plan 700020000002
sections.he:

sections.title: Print Labels
sections.en: 15.3.11 Print Labels You can print the labels of storage conditions with details and paste them on physical samples for quick and easy identification. To print labels, choose Print Labels in Action Box. In Figure 15.27, enter the number of labels you’d like to print for samples in storage conditions. For this example, enter “1” in the first column, select the line item, and choose Print and Change Notification. 15 Stability Study 674 Figure 15.27 Print Labels for Storage Conditions To send the print labels request to the printer spool, use Transaction SP02 or menu path System  Own Spool Requests (see Figure 15.28). Here, you see the list of spool requests for print jobs. Choose the Print Preview icon of spool number 13700, and the screen in Figure 15.29 appears. Figure 15.28 List of Spool Requests © 675 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.29 Labels Printing Note Consider engaging an ABAP consultant (programmer) to develop the layout/format of the physical sample’s label that meets your company’s business needs.

sections.title: Define the Start Date of the Study
sections.en: 15.3.12 Define the Start Date of the Study The start date of the stability study is the formal start of the stability study and the date for the system to automatically create all further testing schedules. In Action Box, choose Define Start Date of Study, and enter the start date for your stability study. Choose Save and Change Notification.

sections.title: Manual Inspection Lot for Storage Condition: Inspection Type 1602
sections.en: 15.3.13 Manual Inspection Lot for Storage Condition: Inspection Type 1602 At any point in time, you can also create a manual inspection lot for the storage condi- tion of physical samples of your stability study. The inspection type for manually cre- ated inspection lots is 1602. In Action Box, choose Manual Insp. Lot f. Stor. Cond., and the screen in Figure 15.30 appears. Here, you see that the system already has Inspection Lot 160000000006 placed under Stor.Cond. 00000001. This inspection lot is the same one that the system created through testing the schedule. Select the line item containing Inspection Lot 160000000006, placed under Stor.Cond. 00000001, and choose Create Manual Inspection Lot And Change Notification. sections.title: Change Storage Conditions
sections.en: 15.3.14 Change Storage Conditions The next available option is to assess whether you can still make changes to storage conditions after the release of physical samples and label printing. In Action Box, choose Change Storage Conditions. At this stage, only a few details of the physical samples are changeable, such as sample location, sample container, and sam- ple quantity. Select the line item for Stor.Cond. 00000001, and choose Save and Change Notifica- tion. If you don’t want to continue with a further stability study of a specific physical sample, you can deactivate or block storage conditions at any time. In Action Box, choose Deac- tivate Storage Conditions and then, on the Lock/Unlock Storage Condition screen, select the checkmark under the Block Indicator column to lock or unlock storage condi- tion(s). Finally, select the line item for Stor.Cond. 00000001, and choose Lock/Unlock Change Notification.

sections.title: Change Stability Study Status
sections.en: 15.3.15 Change Stability Study Status While performing all the steps, activities, and business processes in the stability study, the system correspondingly continues to update its status. The stability study statuses are available near the top of the screen (look for Notif. Status) on the main notification screen. Table 15.2 lists some of the statuses of the stability study. Status Status Description Status Status Description ACTV Stability Study Active SCDF Storage Condition Defined CRIS Create Initial Sample STOR Stability Sample Stored BOMA Bill of Material Assigned CRTS Create Testing Schedule ISCR Initial Sample Created TSCR Testing Schedule Created ISRL Initial Sample Released TSCO Testing Schedule Completed CRIL Create Initial Test STRT Start of the Study ILCR Initial Test Created COMP Study Completed COIL Initial Test Completed CANC Study Canceled DFSC Define Storage Condition INAC Study Inactive Table 15.2 Selected Statuses of Stability Study © 679 15.3 Stability Study for a Material The following are some of the available options in a stability study:  Deactivate Stability Study You can also temporarily deactivate the stability study, if there is any such business need. This may be the case when you want to temporarily put the entire stability study project on hold. In Action Box, choose Deactivate Stability Study. In the ensuing popup, which asks you to confirm whether you want to deactivate the stability study, choose Yes to confirm your decision. A deactivated stability study also deactivates the testing schedule associated with the stability study.  Activate Stability Study Just like with deactivating, you can also reactivate an already deactivated stability study. In Action Box, choose Activate Stability Study. In the ensuing popup, which asks you to confirm whether you wish to activate the stability study, choose Yes to confirm your decision. A reactivated stability study also activates the testing sched- ule associated with the stability study.  Cancel Stability Study When there’s no further need to continue with a stability study, you can cancel it, if needed. When you cancel a stability study, the system locks the testing schedule, as well as the storage conditions of the sample(s). Further, you have to manually cancel the inspection lots. In Action Box, choose Cancel Stability Study, and in the ensuing popup, choose Yes to confirm your decision. For this example, we chose No because we still want to continue with the remaining steps of the stability study.  Complete Stability Study On completion of the stability study, it makes sense to update its status accordingly. In Action Box, choose Complete Stability Study, and in the ensuing popup, confirm your decision by choosing Yes. Note, however, that if there are any outstanding tests or other open inspection lots, the system doesn’t allow their completion unless you complete or cancel the inspection lots.  Remove Stability Samples On completion of the stability study, you can remove the samples of the stability study from their storage conditions. In Action Box, choose Remove Stability Samples to remove physical samples from storage conditions; even partial removal of physi- cal samples is possible. Select the first line item, and choose Save and Change Notification (see Figure 15.34). 15 Stability Study 680 Figure 15.34 Removing Stability Samples from Storage Conditions

sections.title: Display Stability Study
sections.en: 15.3.16 Display Stability Study With this, the standard end-to-end business process of the stability study and the options that it offers are complete. Now that you’ve learned how to set up a stability study and its business processes, we’ll show you how the system displays the stability study information in reports or workflows. Display Object for Study In Action Box, choose Display Objects for Study. This is now the very first item of the Action Box. Here, you’ll find a comprehensive audit trail that covers just about all the information that we presented in this chapter, as well as the sequence of activities that we undertook for the stability study with a material (see Figure 15.35). Tips and Tricks You can also choose the Display document button, located near the top of the stability study screen, to get a view of the stability study document flow. However, the details aren’t as comprehensive as you’ll find in the Display Objects for Study option. © 681 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.35 Complete Trail of the Stability Study Display Stability Study History In Action Box, choose Display Stability History. Here, you’ll find the details of all the results of all the inspection lots that were created and for which results were recorded during the course of the entire stability study. sections.title: Configuration Basics
sections.en: 15.4 Configuration Basics It should be a comfort knowing that the challenging task of configuring a stability study in SAP S/4HANA becomes easy based on all the knowledge and experience you’ve gained while configuring various other areas of QM. The main areas in which the stability study uses prior experience or knowledge are sample management, inspection lot creation and completion, notification creation with the catalog profile, and the information system, especially the info structure. This section begins by covering the configuration options available for the stability study. Wherever the information is previously covered, we’ll refer to the same without repeating the information. This includes, for example, the option to define and assign number ranges to a notification type, the catalog profile, and inspection lot creation from the configuration perspectives. This section does, however, cover the PP section of the bill of materials (BOM), as well as the PM portion of the testing schedule, with ref- erence to the maintenance plan category. © 683 15.4 Configuration Basics Let’s start with the configuration basics of the stability study. The basic data sets up the initial conditions to keep the initial samples of the stability study and includes packag- ing, sample management, and storage conditions. Tips and Tricks To save you the effort of defining all the parameters in any configuration object and also lessen the chances of errors, we suggest that you copy from one of the standard objects available and then make the desired changes to the newly created object. The copy function is available in all configuration objects. Look for the Copy As option.
sections.he:
תצורת ה-stability study קלה בהינתן הניסיון מ-areas אחרים של QM. התחומים המנוצלים — sample management, יצירת/השלמת lot, יצירת notification עם catalog profile, ומערכת המידע (info structure).
הסעיף מכסה את אפשרויות התצורה. היכן שכוסה — נפנה בלי לחזור (number ranges ל-notification type, ‏catalog profile, יצירת lot). אך נכסה את חלק ה-PP (BOM) ואת חלק ה-PM (testing schedule, ‏maintenance plan category).
ה-basic data מקים את התנאים הראשוניים — אריזה, sample management, ותנאי אחסון.

sections.title: Testing Schedule Category
sections.en: 15.4.7 Testing Schedule Category In the testing schedule for a stability study, the configuration that you need to define is to call objects that the system should create on the date of the testing. Some of the call objects are PM notifications, PM orders, and QM inspection lots. Because we’d like the system to create a QM inspection lot on its due date, we’ll cover the desired settings in this section accordingly. To set up the testing schedule for a stability study, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Stability Study  Testing Schedule for Sta- bility Study  Define Testing Schedule Category. Figure 15.38 Maintenance Plan for Scheduling Type Figure 15.38 shows the initial screen to define details of the testing schedule. Notice that the Maint. plan cat. (maintenance plan category) ST is configured for the stability study and stipulates that the called object will be inspection lot creation. The Ref. © 685 15.4 Configuration Basics object (reference object) 0190 stipulates that the basis for trigging inspection lot cre- ation for the stability study will be the physical sample. To the extreme right of Figure 15.38, the number ranges are assigned. The number ranges can be both internal and external. Create new entries as deemed necessary and save.

sections.title: Maintenance Strategy
sections.en: 15.4.8 Maintenance Strategy Because we used maintenance strategy QSTABI in this chapter, we’ll cover its features to enable you to correlate the configuration with business processes. A maintenance strategy defines the frequency with which the system creates an inspection lot (the call object) on its schedule dates. Further, it also enables the business process owner to define the tolerance for early or late initiation or completion of specific inspection tasks. To set up the maintenance strategy for the stability study, use Transaction IP11 or fol- low menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Stability Study  Stability Planning  Strategy  Edit. You’ll see an initial screen to create or change a maintenance strategy. Choose QSTABI, and either double-click the QSTABI field or choose Details. This leads to the screen shown in Figure 15.39. Figure 15.39 contains the strategy unit that stipulates the time unit of measure that the system uses to create call objects. This unit of measure can be in hours, days, months, or years. Figure 15.39 Detailed Screen to Maintain Maintenance Strategy 15 Stability Study 686 A call horizon, defined as a percentage, enables the business process owner to control when the system creates a call object on its planned or due date. For example, a 0% call horizon means that as soon as the planned or due date of the call objects (in this case, inspection lots) is reached, the system immediately creates the inspection lot. Simi- larly, a 90% call horizon means that the system calls the object on a time horizon of 90% from the date of the next planned inspection lot creation. Other available options are how the system should respond when there are deviations between planned and actual tasks, such as inspection lot creation, its results recording, and its usage decision. You can define not only the tolerance for early or late completion in percentages, but also how much (as a percentage) the system should shift in dates when it finds devia- tions between planned and actual tasks. Choose Packages on the left side of Figure 15.40. This screen contains the cycle length, in months, that the system uses to calculate the next time it creates a call object (for the stability study, it’s an inspection lot) on its due date. Figure 15.40 Maintenance Packages

sections.title: Notification Type
sections.en: 15.4.9 Notification Type Because this chapter focuses on a stability study with a material, the corresponding QM notification type in SAP is QS. To view details of the notification type for the stability study, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Stability Study  Quality Noti- fication for Stability Study  Open Stability Study  Define Notification Type. On the ini- tial screen for various available notification types, choose Notification Type QS, which leads to the detailed screen in Figure 15.41 for notification type QS. Notice that the assigned catalog profile enables the availability of relevant tasks and activity codes to notification type QS. It’s also important to note that the Update Group (stats) field is set to 34, which updates the info structure for reporting purposes. We’ll cover info struc- tures in Chapter 18. © 687 15.4 Configuration Basics Figure 15.41 Notification Types
sections.he: מאחר שהפרק מתמקד ב-study עם חומר, ה-notification type הוא QS. ‏SAP IMG • Quality Management • Stability Study • Quality Notification for Stability Study • Open Stability Study • Define Notification Type. בחרו Notification Type QS (Figure 15.41). ה-catalog profile מאפשר זמינות tasks ו-activity codes ל-QS. ה-Update Group (stats) מוגדר 34, המעדכן את ה-info structure לדיווח (פרק 18).

sections.en: 15.4.10 Priority Type The priority type was previously covered during the notification creation section of configuration. Refer to Chapter 12, Section 12.8.5.

sections.title: Action Box
sections.en: 15.4.11 Action Box A highly important aspect of the stability study is to gain a comprehensive understand- ing of the Action Box, which is available to facilitate the business process side. It facili- tates the availability of all common business transactions in one place (in the stability study notification), meaning the user is no longer required to navigate to different screens and options. To navigate to Action Box for the stability study, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Stability Study  Quality Notification for Stability Study  Perform Stability Study  Notification Functions  Define Action Box. On the initial screen to configure Action Box, choose Define Functions for the Action Box, and this leads to an overview of various notification types available in the system. Choose Notification Type QS. Here, the system automatically copies the catalog profile from Figure 15.41. You can add the relevant codes for tasks and activities so that, subsequently, the same becomes available on the notification screen of the stability study. Next, choose Activities in the dialog structure to see the screen in Figure 15.42, which shows an overview of all the activities that were visible in Action Box. Choose the first activity, Create Initial Sample, and then choose Details. The screen that appears shows the detailed view of the Create Initial Sample function. The important information to note is the assignment of the 15 Stability Study 688 function module to the creation of the initial sample. If a company has created a busi- ness-specific function module to cater to a unique process, then the consultant or the business process owner can assign it at this stage. Choose Dependent Follow-Up Functions in Figure 15.42, and you can add a new function for Dependent Follow-Up Function to the function or the Create Initial Sample action. sections.title: Summary
sections.en: 15.5 Summary In this chapter, we covered a series of logical and sequential steps that can be used to cover just about all the business scenarios for implementing a stability study with a material in QM. In addition to highlighting the importance of the QM master data needed to implement a stability study, we also covered the cross-area integration of QM with PP, PM, and MM. Various possible scenarios and their implications on the sta- bility study were addressed. We also covered the configuration steps needed to successfully implement a stability study. A lot of information was drawn from previous experience of configuring and implementing various subareas of QM, such as sample management, inspection lot completion, and notification creation. The next chapter covers the processes in failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) and the control plan. ©

chapters.title: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan

sections.title: Process Overview
sections.en: 16.1 Process Overview In this section, we’ll provide details to help you comprehend the actual steps involved in undertaking the FMEA initiative.
sections.he: הסעיף מפרט את הצעדים בפועל ביוזמת FMEA.

sections.title: Action Plan
sections.en: 16.1.1 Action Plan Companies can take the following 10 steps to chart a step-by-step approach to develop- ing an action plan using FMEA. With the exception of the first step, all the following steps are mapped in the SAP system: 1. Review existing business processes. Examine how each component of the process functions and its relation to the other items. For example, what process is currently in place to receive hazardous materials from a supplier, or which packing material does the company use to pack its fragile products? Use a detailed flowchart for each business process to review the chain of processes. When you review each component of the process with your team mem- bers, everyone gains a greater understanding of the entire process and how the var- ious components are interlinked. Using the process flowchart, you can assign applicable components to the relevant process owners who are performing specific functions in different departments of the company. Assigning applicable compo- nents to relevant process owners ensures accountability and visibility by clearly seg- regating and identifying their roles and responsibilities in the FMEA initiative. 2. List potential failure modes. List all the possible ways a product or process can fail to perform its function. Refer to previous documentation and other records to gain insight into the nature of pre- vious problems and how these were handled. 3. List potential effects of failure. Make detailed notes about the potential effects of failure. The effect directly relates to the failure of the specific process or component to perform its function. While noting details, record how the failure would affect other interconnected processes and functions. © 691 16.1 Process Overview 4. Assign severity rankings to each effect. Rank each effect based on how it would impact the entire value chain. This value chain can be a customer, dependent subsequent operations, or people involved in operating the process. The severity ranking is based on a relative scale ranging from 1 to 10, with 1 being extremely low and 10 being the highest severity. When assign- ing a severity to each effect, you can begin with a standard, general scale and then work closely with other team members to define a specific and relevant severity ranking for each effect. 5. Assign occurrence rankings to each cause. The occurrence ranking reflects the frequency or likelihood that a cause or failure mechanism will occur. Just like severity ranking, the occurrence ranking is also based on a scale of 1 to 10. Review the occurrence frequency by referring to the data and reports, such as the equipment failure record, customer complaints, or even the repair and rework reports. 6. Assign rankings to failure detection. Identify each process- or product-related control in place, evaluate the process of detecting failure, and assign a detection ranking to a failure on a scale of 1 to 10. A detection ranking of 1 indicates that detecting failure is certain, and a detection ranking of 10 means that detection of a failure isn’t possible or that no checks or controls are in place to detect the failure. 7. Calculate the RPN. As directed by the business process owner, the system automatically calculates the RPN, which quantifies the amount of risk of failure and helps prioritize improve- ment efforts. The RPN is determined by multiplying severity, occurrence, and detection. It’s always in the range of 1 to 1,000. The higher the RPN, the greater the risk. 8. Develop an action plan to reduce RPN. Lowering the RPN is made possible by focusing on lowering one or more of its three factors (severity, occurrence, or detection). For example, a reduction in detection ranking is accomplished by adding fail-safe processes in shutdowns, installing alarms or sensors, or ensuring timely preventive maintenance. 9. Implement the action plan. Assign people to each action and finalize a timeline for the completion of actions. A practical approach to adopt is the “who, what, and when” approach to implement the action plan. 10. Recalculate the resulting RPN. Recalculate the RPN after implementing the action plan to determine whether the desired RPN has been achieved. If it hasn’t, it may be necessary to repeat this series of steps or perhaps develop a new action plan. 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 692
sections.he:
עשרה צעדים לתוכנית פעולה עם FMEA. מלבד הצעד הראשון, כולם ממופים ב-SAP:
1. **סקירת התהליכים הקיימים.** בחנו כיצד כל רכיב פועל ויחסו לאחרים. למשל, איזה תהליך לקבלת חומרים מסוכנים מספק, או איזה חומר אריזה למוצרים שבירים. השתמשו ב-flowchart מפורט. בסקירה משותפת, כולם מבינים את התהליך. הקצו רכיבים לבעלי התהליך — אחריותיות ונראות.
2. **רשימת failure modes פוטנציאליים.** כל הדרכים בהן מוצר/תהליך יכול להיכשל. הסתמכו על תיעוד קודם.
3. **רשימת effects פוטנציאליים.** השפעות הכשל. רשמו כיצד הכשל ישפיע על תהליכים מקושרים.
4. **severity rankings לכל effect.** דרגו לפי ההשפעה על שרשרת הערך (לקוח, פעולות תלויות, מפעילים). סולם 1–10 (1 נמוך מאוד, 10 הגבוה ביותר). התחילו מסולם כללי וחדדו עם הצוות.
5. **occurrence rankings לכל cause.** התדירות/סבירות שסיבה/מנגנון יתרחש. סולם 1–10. סקרו לפי נתונים (רשומות כשל ציוד, תלונות, דוחות תיקון).
6. **rankings ל-detection.** זהו כל בקרה, הערכו את זיהוי הכשל, ודרגו 1–10. ‏1 — זיהוי ודאי; ‏10 — זיהוי בלתי-אפשרי או ללא בקרות.
7. **חישוב RPN.** המערכת מחשבת אוטומטית את ה-RPN, המכמת את הסיכון ומסייע בתעדוף. ‏RPN = severity × occurrence × detection. תמיד בטווח 1–1,000. ככל שגבוה, הסיכון גדול יותר.
8. **תוכנית להפחתת RPN.** ע"י הורדת אחד או יותר משלושת הגורמים. למשל, הורדת detection ע"י תהליכי fail-safe, ‏alarms/sensors, או אחזקה מונעת בזמן.
9. **יישום התוכנית.** הקצו אנשים וקבעו לו"ז. גישה — "who, what, and when".
10. **חישוב מחדש של ה-RPN.** לאחר היישום, בדקו אם ה-RPN הרצוי הושג. אם לא, חזרו על הצעדים או צרו תוכנית חדשה.

sections.title: Failure Across Categories
sections.en: 16.1.2 Failure Across Categories FMEA categorizes risk of failure across three categories, including occurrence (how likely failure is to occur), severity (how big an impact it would have), and detection (how likely the failure is to be detected as soon as it occurs): Risk priority number (RPN) = Severity × Occurrence × Detection FMEA uses a 1–10 ranking for each factor, with 10 being very likely to occur, have a sig- nificant impact, or be detected. FMEA multiplies the three individual rankings of those three factors to come up with the RPN. The value of the RPN can be in the range of 1 to 1,000. The higher the RPN value is, the greater the possibility of failure is in a produc- tion or business process. Companies must then reduce the RPN as much as possible to prevent or eliminate failures. Companies can use FMEA in the SAP S/4HANA system to lower their RPNs by taking preventative and detection measures. The team that manages the FMEA predefines the valuation (on a scale of 1 to 10) for each of the three areas mentioned (occurrence, detection, and prevention) and the RPN benchmark that it wants to achieve. The FMEA team then undertakes practical actions, such as making design changes, placing visual signboards, and pasting labels to edu- cate the production or process users to adhere to given guidelines or conduct technical skills enhancement trainings. After performing these actions, the FMEA team updates the valuation of each of the three areas, and the system automatically recalculates the RPN. If the RPN is reduced to the benchmark level, the FMEA team calls this achieve- ment a success. If not, another round of practical actions is put in place, and the process to calculate new or reduced RPNs starts all over again.
sections.he:
FMEA מסווג סיכון בשלוש קטגוריות: ‏occurrence (סבירות), ‏severity (גודל ההשפעה), ו-detection (סבירות הזיהוי):
‏Risk priority number (RPN) = Severity × Occurrence × Detection
FMEA משתמש בדירוג 1–10 לכל גורם (10 — סביר מאוד/השפעה משמעותית/זיהוי). מכפיל את שלושת הדירוגים ל-RPN. הטווח 1–1,000. ככל שגבוה, סבירות הכשל גדולה. החברות צריכות להפחית את ה-RPN. ניתן עם FMEA ב-S/4HANA ע"י אמצעי מניעה וזיהוי.
צוות ה-FMEA מגדיר מראש את ההערכה (1–10) לשלושת התחומים (occurrence, ‏detection, ‏prevention) ואת benchmark ה-RPN הרצוי. ואז נוקט פעולות מעשיות — שינויי design, שלטים, תוויות, הדרכות. לאחר מכן, הצוות מעדכן את ההערכה, והמערכת מחשבת מחדש. אם ה-RPN ירד ל-benchmark — הצלחה. אם לא, סבב נוסף.

sections.title: Closed-Loop Quality Approach
sections.en: 16.1.3 Closed-Loop Quality Approach The ability to create FMEA along with all its components and then integrate it with con- trols in the SAP system provides the added leverage of having all the critical informa- tion in one system (the SAP system). Further, FMEA also provides an option to create an extensive question list that acts as a validation tool to ensure that all questions were eventually validated with the correct/desired answers, and then it becomes possible for a company to achieve a reduced RPN. Figure 16.1 shows a step-by-step FMEA approach 1 in closed-loop quality management. It’s the direct outcome of complaints coming from customers 2 or analytics such as statistical process control monitoring 3 in production processes. Finally, you can leverage FMEA to incorporate important characteristics in an inspec- tion plan 4 for regular and consistent monitoring and control of characteristics that are critical to quality. Now that you have a better understanding of what FMEA is and does, let’s move on to setting up FMEA in the system. © 693
sections.he:
היכולת ליצור FMEA על כל רכיביו ולשלבו עם בקרות ב-SAP נותנת את היתרון של כל המידע הקריטי במערכת אחת. כמו כן, FMEA מציע question list מקיף ככלי תיקוף, וכך ניתן להשיג RPN מופחת.
Figure 16.1 — גישת FMEA צעד-אחר-צעד ‏(1) ב-closed-loop quality management. תוצאה ישירה של תלונות לקוחות ‏(2) או analytics כגון statistical process control ‏(3).
לבסוף, ניתן למנף FMEA לשילוב מאפיינים חשובים ב-inspection plan ‏(4) לניטור עקבי של מאפיינים critical-to-quality.

sections.title: Set Up
sections.en: 16.2 Set Up Figure 16.1 FMEA Workflow 16.2 Set Up You can access FMEA using Transaction QM_FMEA or menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Failure Mode and Effects Analysis  Cockpit (Figure 16.2). This screen shows some of the often hidden (or little-known) or unused produc- tivity tools and options available. Figure 16.2 1 shows the menu bar to create, change, copy, delete, expand, or shrink various FMEA elements. Another menu bar 2 offers options to switch between change or display FMEA, as well as make other relevant settings. With the third menu bar 3, you can attach files, refer- ence documents, and even web links to FMEA. Similarly, you can keep an eye on the alerts and messages 4 that are available at the top-right side of FMEA. Double-click the message icon, and details of the message appear at the bottom of the same screen 5. The final menu bar 6 offers options to view or print various FMEA elements. We sug- gest that you take time to explore the several tools and the menus that we’ve high- lighted in Figure 16.2. FMEA (product/ process) Statistical process control Zero-defect production Inspection plan Control plan Complaints (8D process) Quality notification Critical-to-quality characteristics Critical-to-quality characteristics Characteristics Defects Characteristics Defects Characteristics Defects Characteristics Defects Environment, health, and safety specification 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 694 Figure 16.2 Productivity Tools in FMEA Figure 16.3 divides the entire FMEA Cockpit into four distinct sections: 1 In the navigation area, the system provides the options to create new objects, such as an FMEA or question list. It also gives the flexibility to copy one FMEA item to another, delete an item within the FMEA, or even look for specific information within the FMEA. All these options are available via the icons available at the top-left side of Figure 16.3. Figure 16.3 Structure of FMEA © 695 16.2 Set Up 2 The work area of the screen is blank unless you’re already working on a specific FMEA. 3 The Worklist shows the FMEAs or other objects that you’ve worked on in the recent past and is available in the FMEA Cockpit’s history. To make more space in the FMEA Cockpit, you can hide the details shown in the lower-left side of the screen by choos- ing the Close button (the blue cross). 4 The cross-linking area helps to bring together all the FMEA items in one work area so that you can quickly create FMEA items. This option is especially helpful when you have several hierarchy levels in FMEA and need to create new links or navigate to any specific link. Tips and Tricks We’ll be taking the longer route of explaining each and every FMEA item in this chapter in detail, but you also can choose the Form button in Figure 16.3. Then, you can quickly and intuitively create all the items that we cover in this chapter 5. After reading the entire chapter and understanding all FMEA items, we suggest that you come back to Figure 16.3 to explore the available options and consider leveraging these productivity tools. Choose the New icon in Figure 16.4, and from the dropdown, you can create a new FMEA, a question list, or either of the two using a template. A template is a previously created FMEA or question list that you can use to save time and effort instead of man- ually entering all the details all over again. Figure 16.4 FMEA Cockpit to Create a New FMEA Choose FMEA from the dropdown list in Figure 16.4, and the system brings up the basic data view of the FMEA in Figure 16.5. On the right side of the screen, enter “REVO” for 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 696 the FMEA field (for the rest of this chapter, we’ll use FMEA REVO as an example) and enter its Description. Notice the additional icons right next to the FMEA field that enable you to add additional notes or attachments for reference and record purposes. Figure 16.5 Basic Data Tab of FMEA The option to attach documents or notes is also generally available while you’re creat- ing all items of the FMEA. The system prompts you to select the FMEA type, which can be either System FMEA Product or System FMEA Process. Select the Product option, and enter material number “FG129”. Enter the planned start and end dates of FMEA in the lower half of the screen (not shown). When you’ve actually started and then finally completed all steps of FMEA, you can update the actual start and end dates of the FMEA in the bottom half of Figure 16.5 (not shown). Choose the Texts tab to reach the screen shown in Figure 16.6. Here, you incorporate more details about the FMEA, including adding an FMEA description and notes. You can even upload (and download) the content from some other data source, such as another drive in your laptop, and incorporate it in either the description or the note areas of the FMEA. This is possible when you choose the relevant upload or download icons. In the Participant(s) tab, enter the roles and names of the persons who will be part of the FMEA team. This step enables you to assign responsibility to the relevant persons. Then, in all subsequent status updates or reporting, information on participants helps you find whose tasks are pending or overdue, or even which resource/participant is assigned what task(s). © 697 16.2 Set Up Figure 16.6 Texts in FMEA Tips and Tricks Use Transaction BP in SAP S/4HANA to create or amend business partners (team mem- bers) who will be part of the FMEA initiative. In the Result tab (see Figure 16.7), you can see that while you’re creating a new FMEA, the system hasn’t calculated the FMEA results (the RPN). Later, you’ll see how the sys- tem automatically fills these fields after it calculates the RPN. Figure 16.7 Results Tab of FMEA In the lower half of the screen, in the Valuation Specifications area, the system enables you to select the procedure that you want to use as a valuation specification for FMEA. For this example, use the valuation procedure to calculate the RPN. In addition, it’s 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 698 important to note that you can define the minimum result that the system must achieve for the FMEA. In other words, it acts as a benchmark to compare the actual RPN of the FMEA with the minimum results and enables the system to conduct Overall Assesst. (assessment) to declare the FMEA initiative a success or a failure. Save the FMEA by choosing the Save button located in the bottom-right side of the screen (not shown). Note You can click to the Message icon located at the top-right side of Figure 16.7 to view any error or warning messages. When you choose the message, you’ll see the message text at the bottom of Figure 16.7 (not shown because this example doesn’t have any warn- ing or error messages). Figure 16.7 shows that we’ve created and saved FMEA REVO. In case of a warning or error that may prevent the system from saving a FMEA record, the system helps you by highlighting the missing or incomplete items within the FMEA. It also brings up a mes- sage when you’ve maintained all the information and notes that the information is complete and correct. Note As FMEA is a specialized audit management tool, it’s possible to configure the levels of audit components as well as set other control functions, including how to structure FMEA and set its hierarchy. We’ll show them in Section 16.8. Let’s now create the FMEA items, including a function list.

sections.title: Create Function List
sections.en: 16.2.1 Create Function List To create a function list, right-click FMEA REVO, and the system brings up the option to create a function list (Figure 16.8). Select Functions, and the system brings up the screen shown in Figure 16.9. In FMEA, a function list consists of a list of FMEA items that are further broken down into individual components. It consists of characteristics, their associated failure modes, and the reasons for their occurrence. We’ll cover all of them in the following sections of this chapter. Tips and Tricks You can always perform a consistency check for FMEA by using the available options available. © 699 16.2 Set Up On the right side of Figure 16.9, enter a function list and a short description. In addition, enter relevant text in the Definition area. All of this entered text will eventually be visi- ble in either FMEA or its print preview, which we’ll cover later. As soon as we enter these texts, the system automatically updates this information on the left side of Figure 16.9. Hence, while you continue entering or updating information on the right side of the screen, the system keeps updating it on the left side. Notice that there is a display field for RPN Value, which at this stage is zero because the RPN isn’t calculated yet. Figure 16.8 Creating Functions Figure 16.9 Basic Data of Function List 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 700 Tips and Tricks If you don’t want to manually enter identification details in FMEA items, such as in the Functions field in Figure 16.9, then leave it blank. The system automatically assigns an internal numeric identification to all such FMEA items for which it’s unable to find identification. However, you do still have to enter a description of each FMEA item. Choose Valuation Specifications in Figure 16.9, and the system brings up Figure 16.10, showing the Valuation Specifications of the function list. Here again, because of the correct configuration in place, the system automatically selects RPN calculation as the valuation procedure. In the Catalogs area, enter the Catalog Profile “000000001”, which consists of an indi- vidual catalog and code group. A catalog, together with the code group, enables the pro- cess owner to group or combine similar codes and information within a catalog. For example, the Defect Types catalog lists out all the possible defects that one can encoun- ter in FMEA, and each individual defect is denoted by its defect code. These individual codes are grouped together as a code group: all electrical defects are grouped under one code group, while all mechanical defects are combined in another code group. For ease of understanding and working, we incorporate all the code groups applicable in FMEA. For example, the Causes item has code group 5, so we incorporate it here. Figure 16.10 Valuation Specifications of the Function List © 701 16.2 Set Up Note You can use Transaction QS41 to add or amend any codes or code groups to meet your business needs. Chapter 3 covers how to create a catalog profile and all the associated catalogs, code groups, codes, and selected sets.

sections.title: Create Functions
sections.en: 16.2.2 Create Functions In Figure 16.11, place the cursor on the function list (Functions) on the left side of the screen, and then right-click. The system brings up the option to create functions, as shown in Figure 16.11. Choose Functions, and the screen in Figure 16.12 appears. Figure 16.11 Create Functions Figure 16.12 Basic Data Tab of Functions 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 702 In Figure 16.12, name the Functions as “FUNCTIONS” and add a description and long text to it. As soon as you do this, the system updates this information on the left side of the screen. As already mentioned, the system automatically updates the FMEA tree as soon as you enter or make any changes to the relevant fields on the right side. Choose Valu- ation Specifications in Figure 16.12 to go to Figure 16.13. Figure 16.13 Valuation Specifications of Function In Figure 16.13, due to the necessary configuration in place, the system automatically selects Calculation of Action Priority (AP) and Risk Priority Number (RPN) as the valua- tion procedure. However, you can manually select other valuation procedures from the dropdown list. We’ll cover how to set up the configuration options in Section 16.8.2.

sections.title: Create Prerequisite
sections.en: 16.2.3 Create Prerequisite A prerequisite is a precondition that the process owner must ensure before the start of FMEA. For example, a kickoff meeting takes place to announce the formal start of the FMEA initiative, or the process owners must first be trained and educated on the need to use FMEA to bring about process improvements. In Figure 16.14, right-click Function (on the left side of the screen). In the ensuing avail- able options, choose Prerequisite and then navigate to creating a new prerequisite. On the right side of Figure 16.15, enter the prerequisite, its description, and similar details in the large text box. © 703 16.2 Set Up Figure 16.14 Creating a Prerequisite Figure 16.15 Basic Data Characteristic
sections.he:
prerequisite הוא תנאי מוקדם לפני תחילת FMEA. למשל, פגישת kickoff, או הדרכת בעלי התהליך.
ב-Figure 16.14, לחיצה ימנית על Function (משמאל). בחרו Prerequisite וצרו חדש.
מימין (Figure 16.15), הזינו את ה-prerequisite, תיאור, ופרטים בתיבת הטקסט.

sections.title: Creating a Characteristic
sections.en: 16.2.4 Creating a Characteristic A characteristic is the individual business process that you want to monitor for improvement within FMEA. It can be a physical or chemical property within a product or a process step within the series of business process steps. Back in Figure 16.11, right-click Functions (on the left side of the screen). In the ensuing options, choose the characteristic, and then navigate to create a new characteristic (Figure 16.16). Enter the characteristic as “CHAR: Brake Pad” because we need to moni- tor the diameter of the brake pad to see whether it has a material defect or there is some other fault. Enter short text, and then from the dropdown list, select the Char. (charac- teristic) Type as Process Characteristic. The other available option is Product Character- istic. Select the characteristic Weighing as Critical characteristic to denote that it contributes significantly to an automobile’s safety. 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 704 Figure 16.16 Basic Data Tab of Characteristic In the lower half of the screen (see Figure 16.17), enter the master inspection character- istic (Master IC) as “Char: Brake Pad” and its Plant as “1710” so that the system can inte- grate the FMEA characteristic with QM’s master inspection characteristics (see Figure 16.17). The importance of this integration will become evident when we create a control plan in Section 16.7. Figure 16.17 Lower Half of Basic Data Tab of Characteristic

ב-Figure 16.11, לחיצה ימנית על Functions (משמאל). בחרו את ה-characteristic וצרו חדש (Figure 16.16). הזינו "CHAR: Brake Pad" (ניטור קוטר ה-brake pad). הזינו טקסט קצר, ובחרו Char. Type "Process Characteristic" (האחר — Product Characteristic). בחרו characteristic Weighing "Critical characteristic" (תורם לבטיחות הרכב).
בחצי התחתון (Figure 16.17), הזינו Master IC "Char: Brake Pad" ו-Plant "1710" לשילוב עם ה-MICs של QM. החשיבות תתבהר ב-control plan (16.7).

sections.title: Create Failure Mode
sections.en: 16.2.5 Create Failure Mode A failure mode is a physical or business process flaw or a defect that requires prevention or correction to increase product or process reliability. In Figure 16.14 shown earlier, right-click Function (on the left side of the screen). In the ensuing available options, choose Failure Mode to create a new defect. © 705 16.2 Set Up In Figure 16.18, create a new defect called “FM: BP JAMMING”, and enter short and long descriptions. Figure 16.18 shows only the partial upper view of the item defect; when you scroll down, you’ll see the screen in Figure 16.19. Figure 16.18 Basic Data View of Defect (1/2) Figure 16.19 enables you to enter the severity as a result of this error. The severity is con- figured on a scale of 1 to 10. The higher the severity is, the greater the number should be. From the dropdown for severity, select 10, which is for Extremely Severe Error (not shown, but located further down the same screen), to denote that brake pad jamming (character- istic) as a defect in an automobile is fatal (extreme severity) and must be promptly addressed. Notice that fields such as Effect and Cause are blank at this stage. This is because we still haven’t created these important FMEA items yet. As soon as we create these FMEA items, the system automatically fills these fields with relevant information. Figure 16.19 Basic Data View of Defect (2/2) Figure 16.20 shows that the system calculates RPN when all FMEA items are in place. In the Valuation area (not shown, but located further down the same screen), the system uses the valuation profile Severity, followed by the valuation proposal, which we man- ually select as a fatal error (the same as in Figure 16.19). The difference between Figure 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 706 16.19 and Figure 16.20 is that in the latter, you enter the specification you want to use as a benchmark to monitor severity, whereas in the former, it’s the actual valuation that results from the FMEA initiative as shown in the RPN Value area in Figure 16.19. Figure 16.20 Valuation Specifications of Defect The next step in the FMEA setup is to define the cause that leads to the defect.

sections.title: Create Cause
sections.en: 16.2.6 Create Cause A cause is the reason or circumstances that leads to the defect in a product or process. A cause can be a mechanical fault, an operator fault, noncalibrated equipment, or insuf- ficient checks and balances in place to identify and correct a defect. Figure 16.21 Creating Cause © 707 16.2 Set Up In Figure 16.21, select the cause by right-clicking the defect (on the left side of the screen). In the resulting options, choose Create  Cause. In Figure 16.22, create a new cause called “CAUSE: CALIBRATION” and enter short and long descriptions for it. In the valuation area, define the chances or the probability of occurrence of this cause. For example, due to infrequent maintenance of brake pad alignment equipment, the machine misfits the brake pad, leading to brake pad jam- ming. Figure 16.22 Basic Data of Cause In the Valuation area, enter the actual valuation of the cause and the probability of its occurrence. This is then used in the calculation of RPN. A probability of a cause occurring 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 708 only sometimes may have a valuation of 5. The system refers to this value from the val- uation profile, where it’s already defined. Choose the Valuation Specifications tab in Figure 16.22, and Figure 16.23 appears. In Figure 16.22, the system will calculate the RPN when all FMEA items are in place. In the Valuation area, the system uses Valuation Profile 8000 Probability of Occurrence, followed by the valuation proposal that we manually select as 5 Moderate (the same as in Figure 16.22). The difference between Figure 16.22 and Figure 16.23 is that in the latter, you enter the specification that you want to use as a benchmark to monitor the proba- bility of occurrence, whereas in the former, it’s the actual valuation that results from your FMEA initiative. In principle, the actual valuation from the FMEA initiative should be equal to or lower than the valuation specifications. Figure 16.23 Valuation Specifications of Cause With a characteristic’s defect and cause already in place in FMEA, the next step is to define the preventive action that you’re going to put in place so that the defect ideally doesn’t occur or is at least minimized. Tips and Tricks FMEA also completely integrates with quality notifications (see Chapter 12). Figure 16.24 shows an example of how you can load the objects from a quality notification into FMEA. Figure 16.24 shows Notification 200000010, wherein you can choose the Cause as Missing Component by selecting the available checkbox. Note The option to load notification objects is available when you’re creating relevant FMEA items. Refer to Figure 16.21 and see From Notification Objects, which you can use to integrate a cause from notification Figure 16.24 into FMEA. © 709 16.2 Set Up Figure 16.24 Quality Notification Integration with FMEA

ב-Valuation, הזינו את ההערכה בפועל וסבירות ההתרחשות (לחישוב RPN). סבירות התרחשות לעיתים — הערכה 5. המערכת מפנה לערך מה-valuation profile. בחרו Valuation Specifications (Figure 16.23).

sections.title: Create Preventive Action
sections.en: 16.2.7 Create Preventive Action A preventive action defines the preventive measure that the FMEA team puts in place to ensure reduction or elimination of the cause of the defect. Figure 16.25 shows how to create a preventive action for a cause. Figure 16.25 Create Preventive Action 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 710 Right-click the cause on the left side of the screen. In the ensuing popup, select Create  Preventive Action, and Figure 16.26 appears. Figure 16.26 Basic Data of Preventive Action Here, enter the preventive action, such as “REGULAR AND TIMELY CAL.”, and then enter the dates during which this preventive action is to take place. In the Valuation area of Figure 16.26, we select the Tgt (target) Valuation as 2 Very Low, which we expect to achieve after the preventive action is ensured. This compares with current/previous valuation of 5 Moderately high. During RPN calculation, the system looks for the target valuation, which in this case is 2, as one of the three factors that calculates RPN. Here, select the Occurrence item (not shown, but located down the same screen), which the system uses to calculate RPN. Choose the Status tab in Figure 16.26, and Figure 16.27 appears. Here, the system assigns the system status of preventive action as Created. Later, we’ll show in the FMEA busi- ness process how to update this system status once you’ve actually performed the pre- ventive action and if you’ve been able to achieve the target valuation. The next step in creating FMEA is to create a detection action that’s in direct relation to the preventive action just created. © 711 16.2 Set Up Figure 16.27 Status Tab of Preventive Action

preventive action מגדיר את האמצעי המונע להפחתת/ביטול הסיבה. ‏Figure 16.25 — יצירה ל-cause.
לחיצה ימנית על ה-cause (משמאל). בחרו Create • Preventive Action (Figure 16.26).
הזינו את הפעולה, כגון "REGULAR AND TIMELY CAL.", ותאריכים. ב-Valuation (Figure 16.26), בחרו Tgt Valuation "2 Very Low" (הצפוי לאחר הפעולה), מול הנוכחי "5 Moderately high". בחישוב, המערכת מחפשת את ה-target (2) כאחד משלושת הגורמים. בחרו Occurrence.
בחרו Status (Figure 16.27) — הסטטוס Created. בהמשך נראה כיצד לעדכן לאחר הביצוע.
הצעד הבא — detection action.

sections.title: Create Detection Action
sections.en: 16.2.8 Create Detection Action A detection action stipulates the possibility of detecting a defect or a failure mode. It can range from quick and easy to detect a defect by putting the right tools in place to nearly impossible to detect a defect. This time, in Figure 16.25, right-click the cause (on the left side of the figure), and in the ensuing options, select the option to create a detection action. The Detection Action screen appears, as shown in Figure 16.28. Figure 16.28 Basic Data of Detection Action 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 712 Enter the identification “DETECT: INSTALL SENSORS”, followed by its description. Enter the Planned Start Date and To Be Completed By date of the detection action, and set the Tgt. (target) Valuation of this detection action to 4 High (greater than or equal to 99.9%). It’s important to add here that the system uses the detection results (probabil- ity of detection) to calculate RPN. Finally, the last item of FMEA setup is to create an effect.
sections.he:
detection action קובע את סבירות זיהוי הפגם/failure mode — מקל ועד כמעט בלתי-אפשרי.
ב-Figure 16.25, לחיצה ימנית על ה-cause (משמאל), ובחרו ליצור detection action (Figure 16.28).
הזינו "DETECT: INSTALL SENSORS" ותיאור. הזינו Planned Start Date ו-To Be Completed By, וקבעו Tgt. Valuation "4 High" (≥ 99.9%). המערכת משתמשת בתוצאות הזיהוי (סבירות זיהוי) לחישוב RPN.
האלמנט האחרון — effect.

sections.title: Create an Effect
sections.en: 16.2.9 Create an Effect An effect essentially reflects the damage or loss that results due to the defect in the product or process. To create a new effect for a defect, see Figure 16.29. Right-click Fail- ure Mode: Brake Pad Jamming. In the ensuing popup option, select Create  Effect. Figure 16.29 Create Effect In Figure 16.30, enter “FATAL CRASH” for the effect and enter its short and long descrip- tions (not shown, but located on the same screen). Choose the Valuation Specifications tab to enter the benchmark value for the effect or severity of this defect on the product or process. This leads to the screen shown in Figure 16.31. Figure 16.31 shows the Valuatn Profile of the effect or severity of a defect. Severity is the third and final factor that the system uses in automatically calculating the RPN. In the Valuation Specifications tab, you can specify the ideal or acceptable severity level that the product or process can tolerate. Needless to say, a lower severity results in a lower RPN and thus higher product safety and reliability. Save your entries. © 713 16.2 Set Up Figure 16.30 Basic Data of Effect Figure 16.31 Valuation Specifications Tab of Effect Setting up FMEA in the QM area of SAP S/4HANA entails a lot of steps, including several interdependent steps. Figure 16.32 shows the FMEA structure at a glance for this exam- ple, REVO, and shows how the different FMEA items relate to each other. With this, all the items that you need to create for FMEA are in place. To show you how all the information that we entered so far appears in FMEA, either as a printout or print preview, select REVO in the FMEA field on the left side of Figure 16.33, and then select the Form button. Here, you see that all the information we entered in various items of FMEA eventually becomes available. Notice that the system hasn’t calculated the RPN yet. 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 714 Figure 16.32 FMEA Structure: At a Glance Figure 16.33 Print Preview (Form Layout) of FMEA Let’s now discuss the FMEA business processes.

sections.title: Business Processes
sections.en: 16.3 Business Processes The business processes in FMEA entail a few important steps that will then form the basis for the system to calculate RPN. These steps are as follows:  Valuation of detection action  Valuation of preventive action  Valuation of effect  Calculation of RPN In each of these steps, the process owner specifies the actions taken to detect failure and how this results in achieving the target or desired valuation of the item. In other words, now you can start to fill in the actual and factual information and results in the system after performing the necessary steps to detect failures in products or processes. In the following sections, we’ll discuss each of these steps, before ending with some additional FMEA features that don’t fit into any of the earlier categories. © 715 16.3 Business Processes
sections.he:
תהליכי ה-FMEA כוללים צעדים שהם בסיס לחישוב ה-RPN:
• Valuation of detection action
• Valuation of preventive action
• Valuation of effect
• חישוב RPN
בכל צעד, בעל התהליך מציין את הפעולות שננקטו ואיך הושג ה-target. כלומר, מזינים את המידע והתוצאות בפועל לאחר זיהוי הכשלים.
נדון בכל צעד, ואז בתכונות FMEA נוספות.

sections.title: Valuation of Detection Action
sections.en: 16.3.1 Valuation of Detection Action Refer again to Figure 16.28, which shows the screen for detection action and is basically the same screen that we were setting up in FMEA (Section 16.2.8). Notice that at the very bottom of the figure, the Start Action checkbox isn’t selected, which means that no detection action has taken place so far. We’ll cover this next. In Figure 16.34 1, you can start the first step of the FMEA business process by entering the actual start and end dates of detection action. This should be the actual start and end dates when detection action, such as installing sensors, was ensured. You can also enter the Level of Completion of detection action as a percentage (100%). Scroll down the screen, and you’ll see the Status area 2. Figure 16.34 Status Area of Detection Action In Figure 16.34 2, the default or the current system status is Created, to denote that no detection action has so far been initiated. Choose the Initial Action checkbox to signal the start of detection action, followed by clicking the Open icon 2. On doing so, the sys- tem updates the status to Outstanding 3. As soon as you perform any action, the sys- tem correspondingly updates the status that you can see in the Status tab. The system keeps updating the system status to match the last or latest action performed. Next, update your detection action by choosing the Confirm icon on the right 3. 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 716 Choose the Status tab 1, and Figure 16.35 appears. This screen shows the last performed action or status set as Confirmed. Hence, as the business process owner, keep setting the actual status of the FMEA item (in this case, detection action) to reflect the actual status of an action. It’s important to add here that the business process owner can use the FMEA Monitor to see the statuses of various FMEAs for evaluation and possible action, if necessary. We cover the FMEA Monitor later in Section 16.5. Figure 16.35 Status Tab of Detection Action Choose Set in Figure 16.35, which leads to the screen shown in Figure 16.36. Set the sys- tem status to Complete to signal completion of detection action. Notice some of the statuses available on this screen, including Remove to delete a status that has previ- ously been set or Force Completion to force completion of a detection action when in reality it wasn’t ensured. Figure 16.36 Setting the System Status for the Detection Action in the Status Tab The system updates the status of the detection action in Figure 16.37, which shows the status as Completed. Save your entries. Warning Before you set the detection action status as Completed, make sure to check if the tar- get valuation (refer to Figure 16.28) is actually achieved and you’ve incorporated it in the Basic Data tab of the detection action. Once you set the status of the detection action to Completed, you’ll no longer be able to make any further changes. © 717 16.3 Business Processes Figure 16.37 Status Set to Completed for the Detection Action
sections.he:

sections.title: Valuation of Preventive Action
sections.en: 16.3.2 Valuation of Preventive Action Repeat all the steps for preventive action (refer to Figure 16.26) that we just performed for valuation of detection action. Once you’ve completed all steps for preventive action, set the status to Completed. The last step in the FMEA business process before the system is able to calculate RPN is to enter the valuation of the effect of the defect.
sections.he:
חזרו על הצעדים ל-preventive action (Figure 16.26) כמו ב-detection action. בסיום, קבעו Completed.
הצעד האחרון לפני חישוב ה-RPN — הזנת ה-valuation של ה-effect.

sections.title: Valuation of Effect
sections.en: 16.3.3 Valuation of Effect On confirming in FMEA that you’ve performed the necessary detective and preventive actions to eliminate or reduce the occurrence of a defect in a product or process, the final step is to enter a valuation of how these two actions have (positively) affected the RPN by reducing it. But before we cover valuation of effect on RPN, choose Cause: Machine Calibration (on the left side of FMEA REVO), and then click on the Basic Data tab of the cause to bring up the screen in Figure 16.38. Figure 16.38 shows two of the three factors that make up the RPN: occurrence and detection. Here, after we perform valuations of prevention and detection actions, the system has assigned a valuation of 2.0 to occurrence and 4.0 to detection. In addition, notice that the system still hasn’t calculated the RPN Value yet; it will only be able to do so when the third and final factor, which is effect or severity, is valuated. 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 718 Figure 16.38 Probabilities of Occurrence and Detection Updated in the Cause of FMEA Choose Effect located on the left side of Figure 16.38 (not shown), and the screen in Figure 16.39 appears. Select the Severity as 10 Extremely Serious Error to denote that the effect of this defect still remains high. Figure 16.39 Basic Data Tab of Effect without RPN Next, we’ll show how the system automatically calculates RPN. © 719 16.3 Business Processes

sections.title: Calculation of Risk Priority Number
sections.en: 16.3.4 Calculation of Risk Priority Number In Figure 16.40, we chose FMEA REVO and then the Result tab. The Overall Assesst. (assessment) reflects that FMEA REVO isn’t assessed yet, nor are FMEA results calcu- lated (Result Calcul.). In the Valuation Specifications area, for Procedure, choose 81 Calculation of Action Pri- ority (AP) and Risk Priority Number (RPN), and then select Rating Profile 81 Rating: No Risk, Medium Risk, High Risk. Finally, select the minimum result that the RPN must reach to declare the preventive and detection actions as successful (in this example, it’s 80.0). Choose the Valuate button in Figure 16.40, and this leads to the screen shown in Figure 16.41. Here, the system calculates the FMEA result (Result Calcul.) as 80.0 via the follow- ing formula: Risk priority number (RPN) = Severity × Occurrence × Detection RPN = 10 × 2 × 4 = 80.0 Figure 16.40 FMEA before Valuation 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 720 Figure 16.41 Result Tab of FMEA with Automatic RPN Calculation Notice that the system assigns the rating as 01 No Risk and the Overall Assesst. (assess- ment) as 1 Passed. To gain a better understanding of how the system assigned 01 No Risk and the role the rating profile has in this, refer to Section 16.8.6. Figure 16.42 Status after Executing Valuation © 721 16.3 Business Processes Choose the Status tab in Figure 16.41, and the screen shown in Figure 16.42 appears, which reflects the sequence of steps undertaken for FMEA, including Valuation Exe- cuted. Tips and Tricks As in this example, the FMEA rating was successful: the results met the specification of 80.0. Had the FMEA been less than 80.0, the system would have brought up a provision to manually overwrite the system-calculated RPN FMEA results. This option is espe- cially helpful when the difference between system-calculated FMEA results is very close to the target value and isn’t worth the time, effort, or resources to conduct another round of FMEA-related activities.
