sections.title: Record Inspection Results
sections.en: 18.4.3 Record Inspection Results Figure 18.30 shows the Record Inspection Results app. With this app, it’s possible to record the results of characteristics flexibly and effectively. For example, you can choose multiple inspection lots at one time and record the results centrally. On record- ing results for the inspection lots, the app automatically valuates characteristics according to valuation modes. Valuation modes define the rules for accepting or reject- ing a characteristic and are discussed in detail in Chapter 3. 18 Reporting in SAP S/4HANA 796 Figure 18.30 Record Inspection Results The Record Inspection Results app offers the following valuation modes:  Valuation mode 100 When a sampling procedure uses this valuation mode, the valuation occurs when an inspection plan consists of a sample size and acceptance number. The acceptance number and the number of nonconforming units are compared.  Valuation mode 400 When a sampling procedure uses this valuation mode, the valuation occurs when a code (selected set) is assigned to a characteristic in an inspection plan.  Valuation mode 500 When a sampling procedure uses this valuation mode, users can manually valuate the characteristics in the inspection plan. This valuation mode also applies to char- acteristics in inspection plans that are without sampling procedures.  Valuation mode 700 When a sampling procedure uses this valuation mode, the valuation occurs when the tolerance range is specified for characteristics in an inspection plan. This app also shows long-term and open characteristics from different dimensions: inspection lot, operation, sample, and master inspection characteristic. Long-term characteristic refers to a criterion for which you can also record results after comple- tion of the short-term inspection. Figure 18.31 shows the options to apply additional filters that aren’t displayed on the main screen of an app. To apply additional filters, choose Adapt Filters in Figure 18.30, and the screen in Figure 18.31 appears. The option to use additional filters is available in almost all SAP Fiori apps. © 797 18.4 SAP Fiori Applications Figure 18.31 Additional Filters

sections.title: Results History
sections.en: 18.4.4 Results History Figure 18.32 shows the Results History app. With this app, it’s possible to display the results history for an inspection plan characteristic or a master inspection characteris- tic. The valuation of a characteristic is shown as a graphic for the selected inspection lots to compare inspection results over a longer period of time. The following are some of the other features available in this app:  Only displaying the results history for quantitative characteristics is possible.  In the list, you can use the Settings to specify the grouping characteristics according to which the inspection lot results are summarized. The grouping characteristics are indicated by the suffix (Characteristic) or (Char).  The individually selected inspection lot results are summarized as one aggregated object according to whether they match the grouping characteristics. If, for example, you select only the material and the master inspection characteristic as grouping characteristics, all inspection lot results for a master inspection characteristic and material are aggregated in one row of the list. If you select the material, supplier, and master inspection characteristic as the grouping characteristic, all inspection lot results for a material-supplier combination and master inspection characteristic are aggregated in one row of the list. 18 Reporting in SAP S/4HANA 798 Figure 18.32 Results History Figure 18.33 shows the mean values of a single master inspection characteristic recorded in various inspection lots. The key figures for the selected inspection lot results are calculated at the aggregation level. The results of a row in the list are dis- played as a graphic. This is the run chart of the sample mean values with their upper and lower tolerance limits. Choose Single Values in Figure 18.33, and the screen in Figure 18.34 appears. The upper half of the screen in Figure 18.34 shows the data points in graphical form, and the lower half lists all the inspection lots that make up the data points shown in the graph. You can make a flexible selection from all selected inspection lot results, and the graphic is adapted accordingly. Figure 18.33 Mean Values of Inspection Results © 799 18.4 SAP Fiori Applications Figure 18.34 Individual Results or Single Values

sections.title: Quality Technician Overview
sections.en: 18.4.5 Quality Technician Overview Figure 18.35 shows the Quality Technician Overview app and consists of four KPIs that are displayed as cards. Information displayed as cards not only provides an overview of important KPIs but also allows a quality technician to focus on the most important tasks and to view, filter, and react to information quickly. Figure 18.35 Quality Technician Overview 18 Reporting in SAP S/4HANA 800 The cards show the most important information ranked according to relevance. For example, on the Inspection Lots without Inspection Plan card, you can see the number of inspection lots without an inspection plan in the header—which in this example is 10 such inspection lots—followed by a list of inspection lots that are sorted based on their creation dates. It’s also possible to customize the overview page by rearranging, hiding, or showing cards via drag and drop. To hide a card, proceed as follows:  In the header bar, select the User icon, and then select Manage Cards. Use the switch control to hide or show the relevant card. Select OK.  To reset the view to the default settings, select Restore in the Manage Cards window. You can also apply a filter to the displayed information, which will affect all relevant cards. For example, you can filter the content of all cards per plant or inspection lot ori- gin. SAP delivers a standard filter variant that you can use immediately. It contains some predefined values for the filter bar. It’s also possible to make a self-defined vari- ant by selecting the Select Variant dropdown arrow. You can also customize the filter by selecting Adapt Filters. Here are some additional details about the various cards:  Inspection Lots Without Inspection Plan This card shows inspection lots without an inspection plan, sorted by creation date. Selecting the header or clicking it leads to the Manage Inspection Lots app, whereas selecting an item leads to the Change Inspection Lot screen.  Inspection Lots with Open Results Recording, No Inspection Points This card shows the total number of inspection lots for which results recording hasn’t started or is in process. Selecting the header leads to the Record Inspection Results app. The column chart shows you the number of inspection lots by end date of inspection. Selecting a column also leads to the Record Inspection Results app, but here the inspection lots are filtered based on the end date of inspection.  Inspection Lots with Open Results Recording for Inspection Points This card shows the total number of inspection lots for which results recording hasn’t started or is still in process. Selecting the header takes you to the Record Results for Inspection Points app. The column chart shows the number of inspection lots by inspection end date. Selecting a column also leads to the Record Results for Inspection Points app, but the inspection lots are now filtered based on the end date of inspection.  My Tasks Shows the quality tasks assigned to you that are in either Created or In Process Sta- tus, sorted according to the planned end date. Selecting the header takes you to the Process Quality Tasks app, whereas selecting an item takes you to the Quality Tasks screen. Quality tasks need to be created in the Manage Defects app, and these quality tasks also need to be assigned to the relevant users for them to appear in the My Tasks card. © 801 18.4 SAP Fiori Applications

sections.title: Quality Engineer Overview
sections.en: 18.4.6 Quality Engineer Overview The Quality Engineer Overview app shows the most important information and tasks related to inspection management all in a single page. Just like the Quality Technician Overview app, the information is displayed on a set of cards, thereby allowing a quality engineer to focus on the most important tasks and to view, filter, and react to informa- tion quickly. The cards show you the most important information ranked according to relevance. For example, on the Inspection Lots without Usage Decision card, you can see the num- ber of inspection lots without a usage decision in the header, followed by a donut chart that shows the percentage distribution of inspection lots based on their results record- ing status. You can then decide to make usage decisions for all inspection lots without a usage decision or for those inspection lots with a particular result recording status. You can customize the overview page by rearranging cards and by hiding or showing them. You can drag and drop cards to rearrange them. To hide a card, proceed as fol- lows: In the header bar, select the User icon and select Manage Cards. Use the switch control to hide or show the relevant card. Select OK. To reset the view to the default set- tings, select Restore in the Manage Cards window. You can also apply a filter to the dis- played information, which will affect all relevant cards. For example, you can filter the content of all cards per plant or inspection lot origin. SAP delivers a standard filter variant that can be used immediately. It contains some predefined values for the filter bar. It’s also possible to make your own variant by selecting the Select Variant dropdown arrow. You can also customize the filter by selecting Adapt Filter. Figure 18.36 and Figure 18.37 show the cards that appear in the Quality Engineer Over- view app, and Table 18.2 describes them. sections.title: Manage Usage Decisions
sections.en: 18.4.7 Manage Usage Decisions Figure 18.38 shows the Manage Usage Decision app, wherein you can display inspection lots, as well as manage usage decisions for each inspection lot. For inspection lots for which a usage decision has been made, you can view or change that usage decision. For inspection lots for which a usage decision hasn’t been made, you can make a usage decision. Other key features of this app are as follows:  View inspection lots based on filter criteria, such as the inspection lot origin, inspec- tion lot number, results recording status, and so on.  View and change usage decisions for inspection lots with a usage decision.  Make usage decisions for inspection lots without a usage decision. For this, the fol- lowing options are available: – Make a quick usage decision for multiple inspection lots. This sets the usage deci- sion code that was previously defined as the default. – Navigate to the usage decision details screen, and select the appropriate usage decision code.  Navigate to view detailed information related to a material.  Navigate to view detailed information related to an inspection lot.  Edit the usage decision code and usage decision comments of an inspection lot.  Trigger stock posting of materials of the inspection lot stock to available stock types.  Split the inspection lot stock quantity to be posted between stock types, and choose the storage location for some stock types. You can’t use this app in the context of the following:  SAP Extended Warehouse Management (SAP EWM)  Handling units  Catch weight management  Batch-managed materials Quality Tasks by Processor Assignment  Shows you the number of open quality tasks by processor assign- ment.  The donut chart is divided based on processor assignment.  Selecting the header leads to the Manage Quality Tasks app, where all quality tasks in either Created or In Process status are displayed.  Selecting a section of the donut chart also leads to the Manage Quality Tasks app, but the open quality tasks are now filtered based on the processor assignment. sections.title: Manage Control Charts
sections.en: 18.4.11 Manage Control Charts Figure 18.44 shows the Manage Control Charts app. With this app, it’s possible to display and manage control charts. Control charts graphically represent the characteristic val- ues in an inspection and help detect deviations by comparing measured values against action limits. (See Chapter 19 for more details.) Some of the key features of this app are as follows:  View control charts based on filter criteria such as material, work center, statistical process control criteria, and control chart status, among others. It’s important to note that filter criteria aren’t directly applied on control charts but on recorded results, and the corresponding violated action limits are used to determine how the control charts should be displayed.  Switch between visual filter and compact filter.  Drill down to view action limit violations by inspection end date, chart type, control chart, and inspection characteristics, among other criteria.  Select a data point on the chart and navigate for more information.  Choose data points on the chart to filter control charts. © 809 18.4 SAP Fiori Applications  Select a control chart and perform the following actions: – Calculate and activate – Recalculate – Complete Figure 18.44 Manage Control Charts App

sections.title: Record Inspection Results
sections.en: 18.4.12 Record Inspection Results Figure 18.45 shows the Record Inspection Results app. With this app, you can record inspection results when multiple results need to be captured for a common inspection lot operation. This time-based app aims to offer an efficient way of recording the results of inspection lots. Some key features of this app are as follows:  Record results of inspection points based on their date and time.  Get a scheduled, autogenerated date and time for inspection points. The date and time of the inspection points are suggested based on the time-relevant settings in the routing or inspection plan.  View date and time, status, valuation, progress of inspected and planned character- istics, and valuation history of inspection points.  View long-term and open characteristics. Long-term characteristics refer to criteria for which you can also record results after completion of the short-term inspection.  Check status of inspections.  Check valuation history of the total number of valuated inspection points.  Check progress of characteristics (inspected/planned) based on color codes.  Modify existing dates and times to be in the past or future in the User Fields section. 18 Reporting in SAP S/4HANA 810 Figure 18.45 Record Inspection Results App  Perform different forms of results recording—for example, summarized recording and recording of single values.  Record results for inspection characteristics with the following control indicators: – Sampling procedure – Statistical process control characteristics (note that only recording is possible, but no control chart graphic is shown) – Required and optional characteristics – Automatic defects recording – All inspection scopes – Long-term characteristics – Quantitative characteristics with specification limits – Qualitative characteristics with reference to required characteristic attributes  Accept or reject processing statuses of inspection characteristics.  Make a usage decision for an inspection point by selecting a value under Valuation.  Add remarks (up to 40 characters) to the inspection results.  View and edit the detailed data of a characteristic on the characteristic result details screen.  Add master inspection characteristics not planned in the inspection plan or routing to the selected inspection lot and operation on the results recording screen.  Record the inspection results for several master inspection characteristics for differ- ent inspection lots in a table on a single screen. For example, you can use this feature if you have to inspect one characteristic for several materials. © 811 18.4 SAP Fiori Applications

sections.title: Process Quality Tasks
sections.en: 18.4.13 Process Quality Tasks Figure 18.46 shows the Process Quality Tasks app. It displays a list of tasks that were cre- ated for generic defects. You can navigate to a task to process it further. Note You’ll only be able to use the Process Quality Tasks app after you’ve previously main- tained defect-related information in the Record Defects app. It’s important to note that defects created in SAP GUI won’t appear in the Process Quality Tasks and Manage Quality Tasks apps (Section 18.4.14). With the Manage Workflows for Quality Tasks Processing app, it’s possible to activate the assignment of processor to quality task workflow to create notifications for quality engineers and technicians when they are assigned as processors of tasks. The workflow also creates new items for them in the My Inbox app. Here, you not only can view important information related to each item but can also, for example, claim or forward the item, and navigate to related apps. You can also configure workflows for quality task processing. Figure 18.46 Process Quality Tasks

sections.en: 18.4.17 Inspection Lot Detailed Analytics You may not be able to directly access the Inspection Lot Detailed Analytics app shown in Figure 18.50 by clicking its tile on the SAP Fiori homepage. To access it, first use the Inspection Lot Analytics app discussed in Section 18.4.16 (see Figure 18.49). Then, choose Open In located at the bottom-right side of Figure 18.49 (not shown). In the popup that appears, choose Inspection Lot Detailed Analytics, and this will lead to the screen in Figure 18.50. Figure 18.50 1 shows the initial screen of the Inspection Lot Detailed Analytics app, which can be used to analyze inspection lots for which usage decisions have already been made. Analysis can be based on various categories, such as accepted and rejected lots, rejection rate, skip rate, total number of lots, skip lots, and mean processing time © 815 18.4 SAP Fiori Applications based on time, inspection type, material, plant, supplier, and customer. Other key fea- tures are adding or removing analysis steps and saving the most frequently used analy- sis paths. In Figure 18.50 1, choose the Add Analysis Step button (not shown); the Category popup 2 will appear. Choose from one of the available categories, and it will lead to another popup 3, which is basically another drilldown level of the category pre- viously selected. For this example, choose Accepted and Rejected Inspection Lots by Inspection Type and the screen in Figure 18.51 will appear. Figure 18.50 Selection Parameters of Inspection Lot Detailed Analytics Figure 18.51 shows the number of accepted and rejected inspection lots for each inspec- tion type and is based on a time period of 365 days. Additional filters can be set; if a new analysis is required, choose the Add Analysis Step button located on the bottom left side of the screen with a plus (+) sign. Figure 18.52 shows the list view of the Inspection Lot Detailed Analytics app, which can be assessed by clicking the List View icon. Apart from setting additional filters, options to sort the list in ascending or descending order are also available. The dropdown on the left side of the screen offers options to save, print, or delete the analysis. 18 Reporting in SAP S/4HANA 816 Figure 18.51 Inspection Lot Detailed Analytics Figure 18.52 List View

sections.title: Characteristic Detailed Analytics
sections.en: 18.4.19 Characteristic Detailed Analytics Figure 18.54 shows the Characteristic Detailed Analytics app that you can use to analyze inspection characteristics for which results have already been recorded. The analysis can be based on various categories, such as accepted and rejected inspections, rejection rate, skip rate, mean value, standard deviation, cp and cpk indices, and so on, based on time, inspection characteristics, master inspection characteristics, work center, plant, material, supplier, and customer. The dropdown offers other associated characteristics analytics, such as mean values and under-tolerance and over-tolerance values of mas- ter inspection characteristics. The values of cp and cpk are the process capability indices. The first value (cp) is a mea- sure for the process dispersion (is the process controlled?)—that is, how closely a pro- cess is running to its specification limits relative to the natural variability of the process. The second value (cpk) describes the position of the mean value in relation to the tolerance limits and therefore indicates whether the process is capable. The cpk is an adjustment to the cp, affecting its noncentered distribution. In other words, cpk measures how closely the target values are consistent with normal performance. For a controlled and capable process, both values should be higher than 1.33. In many indus- tries, the minimum requirement for a process capability index is now 2.0 or higher! Figure 18.54 Characteristic Detailed Analytics © 819 18.4 SAP Fiori Applications Tips and Tricks You may not be able to directly access the Characteristic Detailed Analytics app shown in Figure 18.54 by clicking its tile in the SAP Fiori launchpad. Instead, first use the Char- acteristics Analytics app discussed in Section 18.4.18 (see Figure 18.53). Then, choose the Jump To dropdown shown in Figure 18.55, followed by clicking the Characteristic Ana- lytics Quantitative Characteristics mini tile. This will then lead to the screen in Figure 18.54. Figure 18.55 Mini Tiles

Next, choose the details icon located on the far-right side of Figure 18.56 to navigate to the Inspection Operation app. Figure 18.56 shows the Inspection Lot app that you can use to view detailed information about the inspection lot business object. Inspection lots are used to record, process, and manage information for quality inspections. Some of the main features of this app are as follows:  Display information about inspection lot origin.  Display corresponding information according to the inspection type.  Display a usage decision for an inspection lot.  Display information about stock posting. 18 Reporting in SAP S/4HANA 820  Display administrative data.  Display the progress of characteristics at the operation level.  Access the Display Inspection Operation app if the operations are relevant for inspection (see Section 18.4.21). sections.title: Manage Batches
sections.en: 18.4.22 Manage Batches Figure 18.58 shows the Manage Batches app, which can be used to display and edit exist- ing batches or create new batches. Using one point of entry, this provides quick and easy access to batch-relevant information and activities. To enable flexible teamwork, new or changed records can be stored as draft versions in the first place. All users with the corresponding authorizations can find these draft versions using the search or fil- ter options and can either discard the draft changes or continue the work. Some of the key features of this app are as follows:  Search for existing batches: – Search for single batches using enterprise search. – Search for certain ranges of batches using selection criteria and filters in this app. – Define a default filter for the following field: Material.  Edit an existing batch or create a new batch. You can edit batch-relevant informa- tion, for example: – Batch status, such as restricted opposed to unrestricted – Overview of all dates, such as shelf life or best-before date or date of manufactur- ing 18 Reporting in SAP S/4HANA 822 – Supplier batch information if available – Overview of the existing batch classifications – Inspection lots of the selected batch – Detailed information about the batch usage, such as shipments  Use the draft concept for changed or new batches. Figure 18.58 Manage Batches If you create a new batch or edit an existing batch, all changes are saved as a draft ver- sion as long as you don’t select Save. For 20 minutes, the draft version is available. During this period, users with authorization can resume or discard this draft version. If you want to reopen a draft version after more than 20 minutes, the system forces you to discard the draft version. This is because the draft version locks all data used in the batch entry for all users—for example, material data. To limit the time all data is locked, the draft version can only be resumed for 20 minutes. Draft versions of a batch can be found using selection criteria and filters. If you open a draft version, the system dis- plays a warning, asking if you want to resume or discard the draft version. With this app, it’s possible to trigger follow-up activities such as the following:  Transfer stock of one batch of a material to another within a plant.  Get a stock overview of a single material within a plant and a storage location.  Perform further analysis and control options such as calling up the batch master for changing and displaying master data, classification data, and the batch where-used list containing information about the lifecycle of a batch.

sections.title: Supplier Evaluation
sections.en: 19.1 Supplier Evaluation Supplier evaluation makes it easier for the procurement and quality management functions to pursue their objectives by providing clear and comprehensible key fig- ures. These objectives include the following:  Determine the current status of a supply relationship.  Show the supplier to what extent the requirements of the purchaser are met.  Create a basis for supplier selection or supplier exclusion.  Determine support after the request for quotation and extend the supply relationship. 19 Quality Control 826  Determine support for higher weighting of the goods receipt inspection and inspec- tion planning.  Provide background information to conclude a quality assurance agreement. In supplier evaluation, you use main criteria and subcriteria to establish key figures that allow an evaluation of individual criteria and the creation of a ranking with an overall score. Based on these key figures, you can initiate corrective measures and improvements in a targeted and focused way. A meaningful supplier evaluation isn’t restricted to determining the current status; instead, it forms the starting point for ongoing quality improvements. The supplier evaluation is an essential element of quality control. SAP S/4HANA pro- vides flexible tools to evaluate your suppliers. All of these tools meet standards requirements, and you can easily adapt them to meet the business needs of your com- pany. You’ll learn all the important steps involved in supplier evaluation, but the focus will remain primarily on quality as one of the criteria that forms an integral part of sup- plier evaluation. Supplier evaluation takes an intermediate position between procurement and QM because it incorporates the information and criteria from both a commercial- and quality-related point of view. In the SAP S/4HANA system, the supplier evaluation happens in procurement (materials management [MM]) and evaluates from a com- mercial point of view, at least in the majority of cases. In addition, the system extracts master and transaction data from MM, such as material, supplier, and purchasing information records. The system evaluates the suppliers at the purchasing organiza- tion level. The purchasing organization is assigned to one or more plants. Note During an actual SAP S/4HANA system implementation project, both procurement (MM) and quality (QM) teams deliberate and agree on the percentages and weighting by which the criteria and subcriteria will influence supplier evaluation. The supplier evaluation makes it possible to evaluate each supplier by using a quality score. The quality score is a combination of all criteria, letting the system create a hit list (a ranking) of suppliers. You can also consider each criterion in isolation. The sup- plier evaluation isn’t limited to covering only suppliers of materials but also suppliers of services, such as maintenance services and cleaning services. In the following sections, you’ll learn how to configure the criteria and subcriteria, including assigning a weighting and percentage to each criterion and subcriterion. Then you’ll maintain the required master data for supplier evaluation, followed by run- ning end-to-end business processes. In the end, you’ll see how automatic supplier eval- uation continuously updates the quality score of suppliers. © 827 19.1 Supplier Evaluation

sections.title: Configuration Basics
sections.en: 19.1.1 Configuration Basics This section will show you how to make necessary configuration settings that the sys- tem eventually uses in supplier evaluation. Weighting Keys The weighting key is the basic identification to denote equal, different, or unequal weight- ing of criteria. A criterion is the benchmark, such as price, quality, or on-time delivery, that you use to evaluate a supplier’s compliance to the company’s business needs. To navigate to the weighting keys, follow menu path SAP IMG  Materials Management  Purchasing  Supplier Evaluation  Define Weighing Keys. In the screen that appears, weighting key 01 denotes equal weighting, whereas weighting key 02 denotes unequal weighting. Define Criteria To evaluate suppliers, the system provides five main criteria and additional subcriteria. These are the main criteria:  Quality  Price  Delivery  External service provision  Service To navigate to the criteria, use menu path SAP IMG  Materials Management  Purchas- ing  Supplier Evaluation  Define Criteria. In the screen in Figure 19.1, choose Quality under Main Criteria and then choose Subcriteria on the left side. This leads to the screen shown in Figure 19.2. Figure 19.1 Main Criteria: Overview 19 Quality Control 828 Figure 19.2 shows the main criteria 02 (quality) with the following subcriteria:  GR Inspection Determination of the quality score from the quality of the inspection lot of the indi- vidual goods receipts.  Rejection/Complaint Determination of the quality score from complaints against suppliers.  Audit Failure Determination of the quality score from one or several audits. Figure 19.2 Evaluation Subcriteria Quality and Scoring Method Notice the several scoring methods that are available for the subcriteria. Our focus is on the quality aspects of supplier evaluation, and scoring methods 7, 8, and 9 apply to goods receipt inspection, shop floor complaints, and audits, respectively. Other scoring methods apply to quantity reliability, price competitiveness, following shipping instructions, or timeliness of service delivery (see Figure 19.3). Tips and Tricks If you don’t want to use a specific subcriterion for the Quality criteria, then you can simply leave the Scoring Method field blank (which means No Automatic Determina- tion; see Figure 19.3). Tips and Tricks You can always amend the standard settings to meet the business needs of your com- pany by adding or removing main criteria or subcriteria as deemed necessary. In total, up to 99 main criteria and 20 subcriteria per main criteria are possible. © 829 19.1 Supplier Evaluation Figure 19.3 Scoring Methods Purchasing Organization Data for Supplier Evaluation In this step, you maintain the supplier evaluation settings that apply to the entire pur- chasing organization of the company. To maintain the supplier evaluation data for the purchasing organization, use menu path SAP IMG  Materials Management  Purchas- ing  Supplier Evaluation  Maintain Purchasing Organization Data. Figure 19.4 shows the purchasing organization details for purchasing organization 1710. Here, the best score that a supplier can have is 100. The system divides the entire screen into various areas that apply to different criteria of supplier evaluation. Let’s evaluate the parameters that are important from a quality perspective for pur- chasing organization 1710. In the Complaints/Rejection Level area, you can control the percentage of a supplier’s business volume (ShareBusnVolume%) that impacts the sup- plier’s quality scores during supplier evaluation. The higher the percentage defined here, the higher the quality score of the supplier during supplier evaluation will be; therefore, its overall impact on changing the quality score (due to quality notifications’ creation) will be low. In the Quality Audit area, if you select the Average of All Lots checkbox, then the system first averages the quality score of all inspection lots and then makes that average part of supplier evaluation. Other parameters on this screen pertain to price and on-time delivery. 19 Quality Control 830 Figure 19.4 Evaluation Criteria for a Purchasing Organization Choose Main Criteria on the left side to see the screen shown in Figure 19.5. Four criteria—Quality, Quantity, On-Time delivery, and Service (not shown)—will form part of the supplier evaluation for purchasing organization 1710. Selecting the Manual maint. (maintenance) checkbox enables you to manually maintain the quality score of a supplier. This checkbox is also available for subcriteria. This may be necessary in the case of services evaluation scenarios, where how well the supplier has fared in provid- ing the requisite services in a timely fashion can be a subjective determination. Figure 19.5 Weighting for Subcriteria Quality © 831 19.1 Supplier Evaluation Choose Quality in Figure 19.5, and then choose Subcriteria, so that the screen in Figure 19.6 appears. In Figure 19.6, you can define the weighting of each of the three sub- criteria—that is, GR Inspection, Rejection/Complaints, and Audit Failure. In this exam- ple, the weightings are 50, 25, and 25, respectively. The screen in Figure 19.7 appears when you choose Weighting in Figure 19.5. The Weighting Key is 02 (for unequal weighting), with Quality having a 70% weighting and On-Time delivery set to 30%. Figure 19.6 Subcriteria for Main Evaluation Criteria Quality Figure 19.7 Weighting Keys Tips and Tricks Remember that a simultaneous use of the Goods Receipt Inspection and Shop Floor Complaint subcriteria may reduce the quality score twice. The negative, or lower, usage decision score and the quality notifications created influence the supplier evalu- ation. Therefore, we recommend using only one of these subcriteria for supplier evalu- ation, depending on specific business needs. 19 Quality Control 832 The quality score calculation is established from the bottom up, which means that you evaluate the subcriteria first. You determine the quality score of the corresponding main criteria by combining the subcriteria according to the weighting. Lastly, the sys- tem reflects the main criteria in the corresponding weighting in the overall score. Table 19.1 shows an example of how the system calculates and comes to an overall score after automatic supplier evaluation. Columns 1, 2, 3, and 4 are the ones that you just configured in the system. Column 5 denotes the quality score that comes from busi- ness processes such as the usage decision, on-time delivery, or price competitiveness. Column 6 shows how the system first calculates and subtotals 7 the subcriteria before moving up to calculate the individual criterion’s totals 8 and then adding up the crite- ria totals to come up with the overall quality score 9. Note Refer to Figure 19.13 to see how these numbers stack up in the SAP S/4HANA system through automatic supplier evaluation; you achieve an overall quality score of 70.0 here, as shown in in Table 19.1. In real-life situations, it becomes apparent that the calculation of an overall score for the main criteria isn’t critical. Although this particular calculation does allow for a rank- ing (hit list) of the suppliers, it raises the question of the need for a negative rating, which, in turn, prompts you to ask which main criteria or subcriteria led to the negative Crit. Criteria Weight (%) Subcrit. Subcrit. Weight (%) Quantity Score from Business Processes Subcrit. Scores’ Calc. Criteria Calc. On-time delivery 30 59 0.3 × 59 = 17.7 Quality 70 Goods receipt lots 50 90 0.5 × 90 = 45.0 Rejections/ complaints 25 99 0.25 × 99 = 24.75 Audits 25 20 0.25 × 20 = 5 Subtotal Quality Scores 45 + 24.75 + 5 = 75.75 75.75 Total Quality Scores 17.7 + (75.75 × 0.7) = 70.0 Table 19.1 Quality Score Calculation © 833 19.1 Supplier Evaluation valuation. In our daily work and our need to constantly improve the quality of our work, the monitoring of subcriteria is of far greater business value. Warning The objective of this chapter is to show you a maximum number of business scenarios in which quality, as a criterion, influences the supplier evaluation. In reality, don’t select too many main criteria and subcriteria! A small number of criteria will increase the level of acceptance and comprehensibility. Start with a simple approach; that is, use only the Quality criterion with the GR Inspection subcriterion, and make the usage decision the basis of the quality score. Let’s now delve into the master data needed for supplier evaluation.

sections.title: Master Data Maintenance
sections.en: 19.1.2 Master Data Maintenance You need to ensure that the following MM and QM master data exist in the system so that you can eventually ensure the necessary business processes:  Business partner master data (Transaction BP)  Material master record (Transaction MM01)  Purchasing info record (Transaction ME11)  Inspection type 01 active in the material master  Inspection plan for material  Maintain supplier evaluation (we’ll cover this next) For this example, use material RM124, supplier EWM17-SU01, plant 1710, and purchasing organization 1710. To maintain the weighting key for the supplier evaluation, use Transaction ME61 or fol- low menu path Logistics  Materials Management  Purchasing  Master Data  Supplier Evaluation  Maintain. In the initial screen that appears, specify the number of the pur- chasing organization (1710) and supplier (EWM17-SU01) for which you want to create a supplier evaluation. This leads to the screen shown in Figure 19.8. Initially, for a supplier who hasn’t yet been evaluated, the system doesn’t populate the fields for the main criteria, indicating that it hasn’t determined the quality score yet. Enter “02” for the Weighting key (for Unequal weighting), and save. Notice that when you enter “02”, the system brings up the numbers in the Weighting column that you just configured. Tips and Tricks You can use Transaction ME6E for suppliers whose weighing keys aren’t maintained yet. 19 Quality Control 834 Figure 19.8 Maintaining Weighting Key in Supplier Evaluation Tips and Tricks You’ll use a different transaction for supplier evaluation, but you can also navigate to More  Edit  Auto. New Evaluation in Figure 19.8 (not shown). The system recalculates all subcriteria and all main criteria, as well as the overall score for the current data. After performing the automatic reevaluation, the system populates the fields for the overall score, as well as the main criteria and subcriteria with the current quality score.

sections.title: Business Processes
sections.en: 19.1.3 Business Processes You continue to run your business processes as you normally would, and the system keeps updating the quality score. These business processes may entail creating pur- chase orders, receiving goods, and performing quality functions such as results record- ing and usage decision. You also record notifications for defective materials received. Further, you conduct and record the results and usage decisions of audit inspections in the system as a part of your routine business. Note Refer to Chapter 4 to see how QM integrates with MM, including in the procurement process. Chapter 12 covers quality notifications, while Chapter 14 has details on audit inspection. After you do some or all of the preceding tasks, you can proceed to supplier evaluation. © 835 19.1 Supplier Evaluation

sections.title: Calculate Score
sections.en: 19.1.4 Calculate Score For automatic new evaluation for supplier EWM17-SU01, use Transaction ME63 or menu path Logistics  Materials Management  Purchasing  Master Data  Supplier Eval- uation  Automatic New Evaluation. On the initial screen that appears, enter Supplier “EWM17-SU01” and Purchasing Organization “1710”. Optionally, you can specify only suppliers who haven’t been evaluated since a specific date (Not Evaluated Since). Choose Execute. The screen in Figure 19.9 appears, and the system shows the results of the automatic new evaluation. This log provides a comparison of the scores between the last evaluation (if any) and the current evaluation with regard to the overall score, as well as the main criteria and subcriteria. Figure 19.9 Supplier Scores Calculation Note The yellow highlight across any quality score denotes that it’s updated or is the latest quality score. If you notice (as in this example) that the columns Old Scores and New Scores both have several yellow highlighted quality scores, this is because you didn’t save the results of the last automatic supplier evaluation. For an analysis of the results leading to the current supplier evaluation, you can navi- gate to any additional details available. Choose All Logs to see a listing of the scores for each material number, as shown in Figure 19.10. 19 Quality Control 836 Figure 19.10 Individual Log The following three sections will discuss how the quality scores from the usage deci- sions of various criteria, such as goods receipt inspections, quality notifications, and audit inspections, are considered in the automatic supplier evaluation process. Quality Score: Goods Receipt Inspection Choose material QM004 and then Detailed Log, and the screen in Figure 19.11 appears. Choose material QM004 and then Display insp. lots, and the system displays a list of the relevant inspection lots, showing the date of the usage decision and the relevant quality score (QSc) for the particular material, as shown on the right side of the screen. Figure 19.11 Goods Receipt Inspection Lots © 837 19.1 Supplier Evaluation Next, you need to evaluate how recording quality notifications for the supplier eventu- ally influences supplier evaluation. Quality Score: Shop Floor Complaints (Quality Notification) If you want the system to consider quality notifications during supplier evaluation, then you need to ensure that you meet the following requirements:  The quality notification type used should be Q2 (Complaint against Supplier), for which you enter procurement details, or at least supplier details. See Chapter 12 for more details.  The notification’s status should be Complete. On completion of a quality notifica- tion, the system opens a popup, in which you need to select the External Origin radio button. Finally, you’ll see the influence that audit inspections have on supplier evaluation in general and the quality scores of subcriteria audits in particular. Note Refer to Chapter 14 for more about how to create audit inspection lots (inspection type 07), which then become part of the supplier evaluation. Quality Score: Audit Inspection Figure 19.12 shows the details of several inspection lots from the supplier audit, includ- ing the quality score of each one. Figure 19.12 Audit Inspection Lots 19 Quality Control 838 Figure 19.13 shows the new and updated quality score after several more business trans- actions that have a direct influence on not just the quality criteria but also its subcrite- ria. The rounded-off new score is 69. We recommend that you perform an automatic new evaluation regularly, such as on a monthly basis or at the end of a quarter. However, you can always perform an update at any time between these intervals. The frequency with which you maintain the sup- plier evaluation depends on your company’s business needs. sections.title: Additional Functions
sections.en: 19.1.5 Additional Functions There are some additional functions available when you’re already in the supplier evalu- ation submenu, found at Logistics  Materials Management  Purchasing  Master Data  Supplier Evaluation. We’ll discuss them briefly in the next sections. Display Supplier Evaluation Using Transaction ME62, you can display the supplier evaluation. © 839 19.1 Supplier Evaluation Compare Evaluations Transaction ME64 allows you to determine the quality score of a supplier for a material or material group and use the quality score for a comparison among all supplied mate- rials. Changes Each new supplier evaluation is also a change to the existing one. Using Transaction ME6A, you can determine who created a new supplier evaluation and when and there- fore display the previous as well as current values. Evaluation in Background Using Transaction ME6G, you can maintain a job that regularly runs in the background and, for example, performs a reevaluation of suppliers on a bimonthly basis. Tips and Tricks The program name for the background job of supplier reevaluation setup is RM06LBAT, and you can choose the evaluation frequency, such as weekly or monthly. Suppliers without Weighting Keys If you access the automatic evaluation in the background, the weighting key assign- ment might be missing. An assignment of weighting keys is necessary if you’ve evalu- ated suppliers with different weighting keys in the background evaluation or haven’t specified a weighting key. Using Transaction ME6E, you can maintain the background evaluation with the weighting key. Print Evaluation Sheet You can print the document of the current evaluation of a supplier with the overall score, main criteria, subcriteria, and evaluation. You may often send a printed evalua- tion sheet to a supplier to inform them about the current status. Prior to this, the default form generally must be adapted by an SAPscript (ABAP) developer to meet the company’s requirements. Access the screen in Figure 19.14 using Transaction ME6F to see the supplier evaluation sheet for supplier EWM17-SU01 Demo Supplier with the overall evaluation and other details. Figure 19.15 shows the Supplier Evaluation by Quality app available in SAP S/4HANA. Based on inspection lots, the variance score of 30.67 is shown for this specific supplier’s ranking. Other trends and graphical representations are also available from the Trend by Supplier dropdown shown on the left side of the screen. 19 Quality Control 840 Figure 19.14 Supplier Evaluation Sheet Figure 19.15 Supplier Evaluation by Quality © 841

sections.title: Quality Level
sections.en: 19.2 Quality Level Ranking List of Suppliers Accessed via Transaction ME65, the ranking list of suppliers displays a list of suppliers with their corresponding overall scores and the scores for the main criteria. You can select the suppliers for display in the initial screen. You can sort the hit list to display the suppliers in descending order, not only in terms of the overall score but also in terms of the main criteria. If you choose a supplier and then click the Evaluation but- ton, the system shows a detailed evaluation of that supplier for the specified main cri- teria and subcriteria. Evaluations per Material/Material Group Transaction ME6B creates a list of the suppliers for a specific material or material group. Such a list is often useful if different suppliers supply the same material. Suppliers without Evaluation Transaction ME6C displays a list of suppliers for which you haven’t yet performed sup- plier evaluation. Suppliers Not Evaluated Since Transaction ME6D creates a list of suppliers that haven’t been reevaluated since the specified key date. Standard Analysis The system embeds the standard analysis in the logistics information system (LIS). Some of the key figures available for evaluation are as follows:  Quantity reliability  On-time delivery Transaction ME6H is available for standard analysis of supplier evaluation. 19.2 Quality Level The quality level is a data record that contains information on inspection levels for characteristics, inspection lots, and material, as well as purchasing information of the supplier. The quality level is relevant only if you’re using the dynamic modification rule, which determines how you can control a change to the severity of inspections or in fact skip an inspection. In short, the quality level is a kind of reminder for how the system should handle the next inspection. For a scheduled dynamic modification, the system automatically creates a quality level with the next inspection lot. For the first inspection lot, the system derives the inspection severity from the start level of the 19 Quality Control 842 dynamic modification rule. In the inspection plan of a material, you can make a distinc- tion between dynamic modification by characteristic and dynamic modification by inspection lot. In this section, we’ll discuss some of the options available for the quality level, such as updating, manually creating, and evaluating the quality level.

sections.title: Updating the Quality Level during Inspection Lot Creation
sections.en: 19.2.1 Updating the Quality Level during Inspection Lot Creation If you haven’t maintained the quality level, the system will do it automatically during inspection lot creation. Initially, the system sets the evaluation to Acceptance and then increases the relevant counters. Results recording by characteristic has no initial effect on the evaluation. The evaluation might change with the usage decision. Even if only one characteristic was rejected (worst-case rule), this leads to a not OK (NOK) evaluation for a lot-based dynamic modification. Therefore, it’s not the usage decision (e.g., rejec- tion) that influences the dynamic modification rule, but the rejection of the character- istic. For a dynamic modification rule by characteristic, the only determining factor is the evaluation of the particular characteristic. The usage decision updates the quality level according to the characteristic evalua- tions. If you make a usage decision without confirming any characteristic results, which is possible, the dynamic modification rule doesn’t work in the case of a charac- teristic rejection. The dynamic modification rule can only work as intended if at least one characteristic is confirmed and completed with a negative result. Note Refer to Chapter 3 to learn more about the dynamic modification rule, which you’ll now use as one of the quality control tools.
sections.he:
אם לא תחזקתם quality level, המערכת תיצור אוטומטית ביצירת ה-lot. תחילה Acceptance, ואז מגדילה את המונים. רישום לפי מאפיין אינו משפיע בתחילה. ההערכה עשויה להשתנות עם ה-usage decision. גם אם רק מאפיין אחד נדחה (worst-case rule), זה מוביל ל-NOK ל-dynamic modification מבוסס-lot. לכן לא ה-usage decision (דחייה) משפיע על ה-rule, אלא דחיית המאפיין. ל-rule לפי מאפיין, הגורם היחיד הוא הערכת המאפיין.
ה-usage decision מעדכן את ה-quality level לפי הערכות המאפיינים. אם עושים usage decision בלי אישור תוצאות מאפיין, ה-rule לא עובד בדחיית מאפיין. ה-rule עובד רק אם לפחות מאפיין אחד אושר והושלם בתוצאה שלילית.
**הערה:** פרק 3 — ה-dynamic modification rule.

sections.title: Manual Creation of the Quality Level
sections.en: 19.2.2 Manual Creation of the Quality Level The system automatically creates a quality level as soon as it triggers the dynamic modification rule. However, we suggest that you create the quality level manually in advance because you need to specify a different start level than the one preset in the dynamic modification rule for certain material. You can create a quality level only for lot-based dynamic modification. To initially create a quality level, use Transaction QDL1 or follow menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Quality Level  Create. Enter the necessary details, such as material and plant, and the system automatically checks whether the dynamic modification rule is already in place. On the next screen, you can manually set the initial quality level. © 843
sections.he: המערכת יוצרת quality level אוטומטית בהפעלת ה-rule. אך מומלץ ליצור ידנית מראש, כי לחומר מסוים נדרש start level שונה. ניתן רק ל-dynamic modification מבוסס-lot. ליצירה, ‏Transaction QDL1 או Logistics • Quality Management • Quality Inspection • Quality Level • Create. הזינו חומר ומפעל, והמערכת בודקת אם ה-rule קיים. במסך הבא, קבעו ידנית את ה-level ההתחלתי.

sections.title: Evaluating Quality Level
sections.en: 19.2.3 Evaluating Quality Level To evaluate the quality level of material 62 and plant 1710, use Transaction QDH2 or fol- low menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Control  Evaluation of Origi- nal Documents  Quality Level  History. Figure 19.16 shows selected data of the quality level. Notice that the time of dynamic modification (Time of dyn. modific) is at the time of the usage decision. Figure 19.16 Quality Level Evaluation Tips and Tricks We also suggest that you explore the various options available for evaluating original documents, including quality scores, inspection results, history of inspection character- istics, and master inspection characteristics. To do so, follow menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Control  Evaluation of Original Documents. 19.3 Statistical Process Control Each business process is subject to dispersion. However, you should have a clear under- standing of the differences between random dispersion and systematic dispersion: With random dispersion, small deviations occur constantly, depending on the respec- tive process parameters, such as tools, operators, and materials. Systematic dispersion, on the other hand, occurs irregularly and can often be traced to specific influences, such as temperature, corrosiveness, or a tool’s wear and tear. Random dispersion influ- ences processes that are already under control. The entire area of process improvement can be divided into three activities: 19 Quality Control 844  Process analysis  Process monitoring  Process improvement In process analysis, you monitor the process and then make the required settings by using statistical methods, including an examination of process capability. If the pro- cess is stable, you monitor it with methods of statistical process control to eliminate or reduce existing systematic variances. Next, you optimize the process. To achieve this, you use statistical process monitoring methods, in which random deviations occur and you determine what steps or controls you need to take to eliminate these deviations for process improvement. You need to continue iterating these three activities several times to continually improve and manage the process. The following sections will show you how to analyze various data analytics tools avail- able for statistical process control, including charts, quality scores, and histograms, among others.

sections.title: Analyzing Data Using a Control Chart
sections.en: 19.3.1 Analyzing Data Using a Control Chart For process monitoring and improvement, the system offers several methods and tools:  Control chart  Histogram  Standard distribution  Run chart  Ishikawa diagram (cause/effect diagram)  Pareto chart  Distribution chart  Process capability examination Apart from these quality control charts, the system also supports Six Sigma approaches for analyzing measured values and nonconformance data, such as Western Electric rules, capability indicators, trend analysis, and exception analysis. An interface to external tools (e.g., the QM-STI plug-in) for statistical analysis is also available to allow you, for example, to verify a significance test. While evaluating control charts for analysis purposes, a quality chart should help to answer the following questions:  Is it a natural process?  Is there a recognizable trend (increasing or decreasing tendency)?  Are there systematic or periodic fluctuations? © 845 19.3 Statistical Process Control  Are there jumps in the process?  Does the process situation change over time?  Do strong, short-term deviations occur in the control variables?  Is the process stable (no exceptionally strong fluctuations)? If control chart analysis or other quality information shows that the process isn’t yield- ing the desired results, then you need to change the process, or suitable corrective or preventive actions should be put in place to achieve a stable and controlled process.

sections.title: Quality Chart
sections.en: 19.3.2 Quality Chart The use of quality control charts forms the basis of statistical process control. Statistical process control allows you to analyze, monitor, control, and improve processes. Qual- ity control charts date back to a technique that was developed by Walter A. Shewhart (1891–1967) in 1924. In general, you use a control chart to monitor the production process. You can soon determine whether a process is under control or how changes in processes or para- meters influence the process. You can also use control charts in the procurement process—for example, for several goods receipt inspections according to the schedul- ing agreement with regular releases. In this case, the control chart can indicate whether the procurement process was under control. In an actual business scenario, the critical measurement items are set, a sample of the same size is taken at regular intervals, the control variable is determined by measurement and calculation, and the control vari- able is entered graphically into the control chart. The typical control variables include the following:  Mean value x  Standard deviations  Range R  Median  Original value  Number of defective parts  Number of defects You can select each control variable as a track for a control chart. If you select two con- trol variables, you get a dual-track control chart. A typical example of a dual-track con- trol chart is the x/s control chart (mean value and standard deviation). Depending on the control chart type, you can set a center line, tolerance, warning, and action limits. The system calculates the warning and action limits during a preliminary phase under real process conditions, and they are entered in the control chart. 19 Quality Control 846 The classic types of control charts for quantitative (variable) characteristics include the following:  Acceptance chart (e.g., mean-value chart with tolerance) Focuses on tolerance; gives you upper and lower control and warning limits.  Shewhart chart (e.g., standard deviation chart) Uses internal process parameters without considering tolerance limits. The following are typical control chart types for attributive (countable) characteristics:  P-chart (fraction) For defective units.  Np-chart For constant sample size. The lifecycle of a control chart proceeds as follows: 1. Creating the control chart for the first inspection lot 2. Creating the inspection points and recording results 3. Calculating action limits 4. Creating additional inspection lots, inspection points, and inspection results 5. Violation of action limits with quality notifications and SAP Business Workflow 6. Violation of action limits with automatic defects recording 7. Closing the control chart 8. Automatic creation of a control chart for the next inspection lot The following control chart types are available for inspection characteristics:  Mean value chart with tolerances (acceptance chart)  Mean value chart without tolerances (Shewhart chart)  Standard deviation chart (Shewhart chart)  Moving mean-value chart  EWMA chart (for mean values with exponential weighting)  Original value and moving range chart for sample size n = 1  Np-chart for the number of nonconforming units  P-chart for the fraction of nonconforming units  C-chart for the number of defects  U-chart for the number of defects for each sample unit

sections.title: QM Master Data Checklist
sections.en: 19.3.3 QM Master Data Checklist The following is the master data setup checklist that you need to ensure is met so that you can start using control charts: © 847 19.3 Statistical Process Control 1. Ensure that the master inspection characteristics (Transaction QS21) has the SPC Characteristic and Sampling Procedure checkboxes selected. 2. Create a sampling procedure (Transaction QDV1), for which you can choose any sam- pling type, such as fixed sample or 100% inspection. However, for valuation mode, choose 800 SPC Inspection. When you do this (and continue with the next screen), the system asks you for the control chart type. You can choose one of the several available control chart types, such as Shewhart (various types), acceptance chart (various types), EWMA-chart/USA, or moving average chart/USA. Tips and Tricks To effectively use and get the required results from each chart type, there are several controls that you need to maintain for a master inspection characteristic. To know which chart type will require the necessary controls for the master inspection charac- teristic, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sampling, SPC  Statistical Process Control  Define Control Chart Type. Here, choose a control chart type—for example, 110 (Shewart Chart for X Bar)—and double- click it. You’ll see several checkboxes already selected and radio buttons that you need to ensure are also chosen at the time of creating the master inspection characteristic for statistical process control inspection. 3. Maintain an inspection plan (Transaction QP01) for the material in which you main- tain the master inspection characteristic. In the SPC Criterion field for the master inspection characteristic, you can choose from the several options available in the dropdown, including Task List Characteristic, Master Inspection Characteristic, Planned Characteristic, Task List Characteristic/Purchase Document, and Task List/ Material/Supplier. Selecting a specific statistical process control criterion depends on your business need for using the master inspection characteristic in procure- ment, production, or sales processes. Run your business processes as you normally would, such as running procurement or production processes, for which you record results and make usage decisions. Mean- while, the system automatically starts accumulating and collecting statistical process control data, which is then available in control charts. Recall that at the beginning of this chapter, you ran the supplier evaluation process. You use the same data (master data and transaction data) to create and evaluate control charts. To create and analyze data of a control chart, use Transaction QGC1 or follow menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Control  Control Chart  For Inspection Lot (see Figure 19.17 and Figure 19.18). 19 Quality Control 848 Figure 19.17 Initial Screen of Control Chart (1/2) Figure 19.18 Initial Screen of Control Chart (2/2) © 849 19.3 Statistical Process Control Note While this example shows accessing a control chart for an inspection lot, you can use Transaction QGC2 for an inspection characteristic and Transaction QGC3 for a master inspection characteristic. In Figure 19.17 and Figure 19.18, you can choose from a large number of parameter selec- tion options, such as Material, Plant, Supplier, Insp. Lot Origin, or even Control chart type. You can also use Dynamic Selections, which has another long list of parameter selection options to choose from. In the Control charts area, the system defaults the Status of control charts to 3 (for Active). However, when you’re working with a new con- trol chart for the first time, the system maintains the control chart’s status as 1 (for New). Therefore, maintaining option 3 for Status of Control Charts doesn’t bring up any control chart. To prevent this, you must remove any entry in this field. Tips and Tricks You can also use these control charts if you want to leverage Western Electric rules to improve and optimize your business processes. Apart from showing where the control limits have been exceeded, control charts can indicate that a process may be running out of control on the basis of an unusual pattern. Runs or trends are examples of these types of unusual patterns, and the Western Electric rules can help detect such patterns. On the selection screen (refer to Figure 19.17 again), you can decide which of the follow- ing you want to proceed with:  The testing of Western Electric rules is to be performed immediately, so all control charts and selection criteria will be checked.  You want to receive a list of control charts, so choose one control chart from the list on which to perform a check. The system displays violations of Western Electric rules in a list alongside the chart number, track, and sample number. From this list, you can branch to the inspection results to display detailed information and to view the control chart. Here is a list of how Western Electric rules display the data:  One point outside of control limits  Two of three consecutive points outside of 2/3 of the control limits  Four of five consecutive points outside 1/3 of the control limits  Eight consecutive points above or below the center line (run)  Fifteen consecutive points within 1/3 of control limits  Six consecutive points in ascending/descending order (trend) 19 Quality Control 850 Tips and Tricks If you no longer have a business need to use a specific control chart, you can set its sta- tus to 5 (Complete) by choosing Close control chart (the lock icon). This may be the case specifically when you want to use a different control chart type in the sampling proce- dure. When you change the control chart type in the sampling procedure, the system automatically creates a new control chart and set its status to 1 (New). To unlock an already closed control chart, simply choose the relevant control chart and then choose Activate control chart. First, select Control Chart 108, and then choose Call control chart in the upper half of the screen in Figure 19.19 so that the lower half of the screen appears. Figure 19.19 Quality Chart: Graphical Representation Notice the toolbar available on the top-left side, which you can leverage to obtain valu- able insights into the details of the control charts and how they calculate the results. The run chart is a simple method to show time-related trends. The system displays planned and actual values, as well as the upper and lower tolerance limits, as colored lines. If you right-click in the graphic, a context menu appears that allows you to fur- ther process the display, such as choosing the desired chart type and controlling how and in what way the data and text appear. Choose Calculate Control Limits (Figure 19.19) (it’s the second icon [calculator icon] from the left side of the toolbar). Here, the system shows the tolerance (upper and lower specification limits) set for the master inspection characteristic and how these differ or vary with control limits. The system denotes these control limits with various colors in Figure 19.19. © 851 19.3 Statistical Process Control Tips and Tricks In addition to other evaluation options, you can download the full data of a control chart by choosing the download option shown in Figure 19.19 and then choosing QM- STI Evaluation (it’s the third icon from the right).

sections.title: Process Capability
sections.en: 19.3.4 Process Capability Figure 19.20 shows the Manage Control Charts app available in SAP S/4HANA with an overview of various control charts. The top half of the figure is a graphical representa- tion of various control charts and chart types that were previously discussed in this sec- tion. The lower half of the screen lists different control charts. As with other SAP Fiori apps, it’s possible to manipulate the data and information displayed here, as well as set filters accordingly. Figure 19.20 Manage Control Charts App This screen shows the process capability, in which the system determines the mean value and standard deviation, as well as cp and cpk values, provided that you’ve main- tained the planned value and tolerance limits for the characteristic. These values are the process capability indices. The first value (cp) is a measure for the process disper- sion (is the process controlled?)—that is, how closely a process is running to its specifi- cation limits relative to the natural variability of the process. The second value (cpk) describes the position of the mean value in relation to the toler- ance limits and therefore indicates whether the process is capable. The cpk is an adjust- ment to the cp affecting its noncentered distribution. In other words, cpk measures how closely the target values are consistent with normal performance. For a controlled and capable process, both of these values should be higher than 1.33. In many industries, the minimum requirement for a process capability index is now 2.0 19 Quality Control 852 or higher! Clicking the forward arrow at the far-right side of the screen in Figure 19.20 will show the details of the selected control chart. Figure 19.21 shows the process capability indices—Cp and Cpk—and their associated values. These values are based on five partial samples with 25 readings. It also shows the fraction of nonconfirming units compared to the overall sample size. Scrolling down or clicking various tabs will bring up additional information for this chart type, which is 166 (Shewhart Chart for P/Samples/USA) as shown in Figure 19.22. Figure 19.21 Fraction of Nonconforming Units Figure 19.22 Mean Values in the Control Chart Figure 19.23 shows the chart type 165 (Shewhart chart for P/USA) with the standard devi- ations of units that either stay under or cross the defined control limits. As with all con- trol charts, it’s possible to recalculate or even complete the control charts by clicking the relevant options, as shown at the top-right side of Figure 19.23. Figure 19.23 Standard Deviations © 853 19.3 Statistical Process Control Figure 19.24 shows the statistical information in data form. It contains not only the mean values but also the standard deviations between the mean values and actual val- ues. Figure 19.24 Statistical Information

sections.title: History of Quality Scores
sections.en: 19.3.5 History of Quality Scores You learned in Chapter 3 that in the quality inspection business process, a usage deci- sion is the last step. This is why it’s often referred to as the inspection lot completion even though the inspection is already completed with the confirmation and comple- tion of all characteristic results. However, an inspection lot disappears from the work- list only after you make a usage decision for the inspection lot. In addition to completing the inspection lot via the usage decision, follow-up functions are automat- ically or manually triggered or can optionally be initiated. For example, the usage deci- sion directly influences the supplier evaluation and quality level, and the system also updates the quality information system. Entering the usage decision code also ensures that it has a quality score that you defined in the usage decision catalog. Figure 19.25 Quality Scores 19 Quality Control 854 This section highlights the importance of quality scores and how evaluating them over a given time period can help with better and more informed decisions, as well as imple- menting and improving quality controls. To evaluate the history of original quality scores, use Transaction QGA1 or follow menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Control  Evaluation of Original Docu- ments  History or Original Scores. Figure 19.25 appears after you enter the data on the initial parameters screen that includes plant 1710 and choose Execute. Notice the large deviation and fluctuation in quality scores, which can help a com- pany decide whether it should continue its business relationship with a supplier. sections.title: Histogram
sections.en: 19.3.6 Histogram Another useful evaluation tool, available in the standard system without any special settings, is the graphic display of variable measurement values in the form of a histo- gram. Prerequisites for the use of the histogram are the variable recording of character- istic results as individual or classed values, as well as the maintenance of tolerance limits and planned values. Managing a control chart isn’t required for using the histo- gram. The histogram classification for individual values is calculated through an inter- nal algorithm. If the inspection results have already been recorded as classed inspection results, this classification will be used as the histogram basis.

sections.title: Summary
sections.en: 19.4 Summary In this chapter, you evaluated several quality control tools that weren’t covered in other chapters. First, you undertook the necessary configuration for supplier evalua- tion, with a focus on quality as one of the criteria for evaluation. The quality criteria had three subcriteria—namely, goods receipt inspections, complaints (notifications), and quality audit. You calculated new scores through automatic supplier evaluation and then evaluated the additional options available. Then, the quality level required you to have a working dynamic modification rule already in place. Finally, you gained an understanding of what it takes to set up and run statistical process control using qual- ity control charts and the tools they offer to help you improve your quality controls. The next chapter covers Document Management System (DMS). ©

sections.title: Configuration Steps
sections.en: 20.1 Configuration Steps Let’s begin with the configuration details, which is the control data node. The control data configuration node of DMS primarily controls important DMS elements such as the number ranges and their assignments to document types. A document type itself holds vast controls, including the SAP objects that it can link to the entire lifecycle of a document and the fields available for changes after the document info record attains a certain status. Here, status type is another important control that prompts or prevents the business user from performing certain functions or actions. Let’s start by defining the number ranges for the document types.

sections.title: Define a New Number Range
sections.en: 20.1.1 Define a New Number Range The first configuration step in DMS is defining number ranges to be used for document info records. When a document info record is created and saved in the SAP S/4HANA system, the system should be able to assign it a unique and incremental number from the number range defined in this step. There can be external or internal document numbers. With external document numbers, the user manually assigns a number to the document info record. Internal document numbers are assigned by the system. The number range is 20 characters long. An important advantage of DMS is the ability to make mixed number assignments, that is, internal as well as external numbers. When a user assigns an external number to a document info record, the system auto- matically adds an internal number to it. During the course of a DMS implementation, the client and the DMS expert agree and decide on what numbers and ranges of numbers are allowed. After the number ranges are defined, these are then assigned to the document types that we’ll discuss in the next section. To define a new number range for a document info record, follow the menu path SAP IMG  Cross-Applications Components  Document Management  Control Data  Define Number Ranges for Document Numbers. A list of existing number ranges, shown in Figure 20.1, will appear. © 857 20.1 Configuration Steps Figure 20.1 Available Number Ranges To create a new number range interval, select Insert Line, as shown in Figure 20.1, and insert a new number range (for this example, enter “07”). Define the identifier as “07”, and then define the number range From No. as “100000” and To Number as “999999” (after checking that the number range doesn’t already exist in the Existing Number Ranges list). Choose Continue and then save. The new interval just defined will show up in the Intervals list (see Figure 20.2). As discussed previously, there are two types of number ranges, internal and external. An internal number range is used by the SAP S/4HANA system for assigning document info record numbers. An external number range is available for users to assign docu- ment info record numbers to document info records. To denote an external number range, select the External checkbox. Figure 20.2 Defining a New Number Range

sections.title: Defining the Document Type
sections.en: 20.1.2 Defining the Document Type Defining and configuring document types is one of the important configuration steps in DMS. The document type is highly relevant to business users and is the first thing they select when creating a document info record. A document type (denoted with three alphanumeric characters) holds a large number of associated controls and func- tionalities, including the following: 20 Document Management System 858  Status networks  Additional attributes used for searching  Object linking  Conversion processes for creating neutral files  Security through roles and authorizations During a DMS implementation, a lot of discussion and deliberation takes place between the DMS expert and the client’s business users to maintain a fine balance of defining document types that meet the business requirements and reporting needs. This fine balance ensures that not too many or too few configuration objects, which, in this case, refer to the document types, are created. Creating too many configuration objects becomes confusing and cumbersome for business users to enter or maintain all the data. Creating too few configuration objects risks losing the depth and breadth required to truly benefit from DMS. To create a new document type, use Transaction DC10 or follow the menu path SAP IMG  Cross-Applications Components  Document Management  Control Data  Define DMS Document Types (see Figure 20.3). The document type configuration consists of the following three steps: 1. Create the initial document type. 2. Define the status network. 3. Define which object links are relevant for the document type. Figure 20.3 shows several document types available in the standard SAP S/4HANA sys- tem. To create a new document type, we recommend copying an existing document type to save time and maintenance. For this example, use the standard available docu- ment type DRW to create a new document type QM1. Select document type DRW, and choose the Copy As function in the menu bar. Figure 20.3 Available Document Types © 859 20.1 Configuration Steps As shown in Figure 20.4, enter the new Document Type “QM1”, and maintain a short description in the Doc. Type Desc. field. Maintain the Internal Number Range “07” that was defined in the previous configuration step in Figure 20.5.
